question: What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient?

options.C: reassurance with referral to a migraine specialist
options.D: CT of the head and orbits

explanation: This patient demonstrates a classic presentation of acute idiopathic blind-spot (IBS) syndrome. IBS syndrome typically is monocular, occurs more frequently in young women and presents with an enlarged blind spot scotoma and adjacent photopsias. Some have described IBS syndrome as a "waste basket" diagnosis because it probably includes numerous other diagnoses with subtle exam findings such as multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) and acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR). In MEWDS, for instance, the presentation is nearly identical to IBS syndrome but there are characteristic small white dots on fundus exam. These small white dots only last days to weeks and can disappear before seen on examination. If the white dots are seen, the diagnosis made will likely be MEWDS. If a normal fundus is seen, the diagnosis made will likely be IBS syndrome. Similarly, AZOOR has a nearly identical presentation and is characterized by chorioretinal atrophy and pigment clumping around the optic nerve in the weeks to months after onset. In all of these syndromes, a multifocal ERG often shows focal areas of retinal dysfunction corresponding to the region of the patient's scotoma. While in theory this could be a presentation of optic neuritis prompting possible intravenous steroid treatment, the lack of pain and afferent pupillary defect make that diagnosis exceedingly unlikely. If one were to evaluate the patient for optic neuritis or other signs of demyelinating white matter disease, the scan of choice would be an MRI of the brain and orbits with and without IV contrast (not a CT of the brain and orbits). While this could simulate a scintillating scotoma of a migraine, migraine auras typically last 5 to 60 minutes and are usually associated with headache within an hour of the aura onset (though headache does not have to be present). 30-year-old Caucasian female presents with 1 week of malaise, fevers, bilateral facial palsy, and photophobia. Your examination shows bilateral non-granulomatous uveitis and the external exam findings displayed above. What is the name of the syndrome that this patient displays? A.Heerfordt syndrome B.Lofgren syndrome C.Raymond syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient displays the classic findings of Heerfordt syndrome (aka uveoparotid fever): uveitis, facial palsy (usually from parotid gland involvement / swelling as seen in this photo), and fever. Heerfordt syndrome is one of many ways that sarcoidosis can present. This particular presentation is not pathognomonic of sarcoidosis and the diagnosis must still be proven by excluding alternative etiologies and obtaining a biopsy sample that demonstrates granulomatous inflammation typical of sarcoid. Lofgren syndrome is another specific presentation of sarcoid characterized by the triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy (usually diagnosed on chest imaging), and arthritis. Raymond syndrome and Claude syndrome are brainstem syndromes that are not specific for any one etiology but rather represent a constellation of findings attributable to a lesion affecting certain structures in the brainstem. Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasiculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), what percentage of patients with optic neuritis suffered from periocular pain in association with the optic neuritis attack? A.12% B.52% C.72% D.92% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial showed that 92% of optic neuritis cases have associated periocular pain. Due to this relatively-sensitive symptom, an absence of pain should raise doubt regarding the diagnosis of optic neuritis. A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset diplopia. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus but reports no ocular history. Vision is 20/20 in both eyes and the anterior and posterior examination demonstrates no abnormalities. Motility examination demonstrates a complete left third nerve palsy. The patient undergoes immediate workup including MRI / MRA brain which demonstrates an acute infarction of the left cerebral peduncle. Which of the following additional examination findings would be expected? A.Right sided hemiparesis B.Right sided ataxia C.Left sided contralateral tremor and involuntary limb movements D.Convergence retraction saccades High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: An infarction of the cerebral peduncle with involvement of the third nerve fascicle is known as Weber syndrome. The nucleus of the third nerve is located in the dorsal midbrain and contains the subnuclei whose projecting fibers are destined for the bilateral levator palpebrae superioris muscles, ipsilateral medial rectus, ipsilateral inferior rectus, ipsilateral pupillary sphincter (via parasympathetics), and the contralateral superior rectus. A lesion involving the nucleus would therefore lead to a bilateral levator and superior rectus palsy and a complete ipsilateral third nerve palsy (see image). The projecting fibers (fascicle) then traverse ventrally passing near or through the red nucleus, substantia nigra, and cerebral peduncle to exit the midbrain. A lesion involving the fascicle and surrounding structures can produce a unilateral third palsy in addition to contralateral neurological signs based on the location; fascicular palsies may also be isolated. Historically, these lesions have been classified into several syndromes which have considerable variability in the literature, except for Weber syndrome which is consistently a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. Therefore, it is more useful to recognize the location of the lesion and resultant findings rather than the name of the syndrome. These lesions are classified as such: 1. Lesion of the cerebral peduncle: Contralateral hemiparesis due to involvement of the corticospinal tract within the cerebral peduncle (Weber syndrome) 2. Lesion of the red nucleus and substantia nigra: Contralateral ataxia or tremor / involuntary limb movements (Benedikt syndrome) 3. Lesion of decussating fibers from the superior cerebellar peduncle in the dorsal midbrain: Contralateral ataxia (Claude syndrome) 4. Dorsal midbrain lesion: CN III fascicular lesion + ipsilateral ataxia +/- some features of dorsal midbrain syndrome (e.g., vertical gaze paresis, convergence retraction saccades, skew deviation, and lid retraction) (Nothnagel syndrome) The typical cause of these syndromes is infarction in the territory of a paramedian penetrating vessel arising from the proximal posterior cerebral artery. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice B): A contralateral ataxia would be possible in one of the other three syndromes, but involvement of only the cerebral peduncle should not produce a contralateral ataxia. • (Choice C): Common to all of these syndromes is an ipsilateral third nerve palsy in addition to contralateral neurologic signs. • (Choice D): Convergence retraction saccades can be found in a dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not be expected in a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. REFERENCE: Liu GT, Crenner CW, Logigian EL, Charness ME, Samuels MA. Midbrain syndromes of Benedikt, Claude, and Nothnagel: setting the record straight. Neurology. 1992 Sep;42(9):1820-2.

question: In which clinical scenario is a visual evoked potential (VEP) a useful test?

options.A: a 35-year-old male with a history of bilateral optic neuritis and multiple embolic infarcts to both occipital lobes has decreased vision OU on exam with normal color plate testing and nerve fiber layer thickness on OCT OU. A flash VEP is ordered to distinguish the cause of his decreased vision.
options.B: a 48-year-old female with a history of numerous episodes of neurologic dysfunction (loss of sensation, loss of taste, shooting sensations) usually lasting less than a day. She now presents with blurred vision. The MRI of the brain is normal and a pattern reversal VEP is ordered to rule out multiple sclerosis induced visual disturbance.
options.C: a 10-year-old cognitively-delayed non-verbal boy is brought in by his parents for an eye check. His parents want to know how much he can see. A pattern reversal VEP is ordered to provide a rough estimate of the child's visual function.
options.D: a 45-year-old woman is struck in the head while at work and claims bilateral count fingers vision with severe photophobia despite an otherwise normal exam. She is very uncooperative on exam (always blinking and refusing to open her eyes). A pattern- reversal VEP is ordered to prove that she has functional vision loss.

explanation: Visually evoked potentials are rarely useful clinically. A VEP is performed by presenting a visual stimulus to one eye (e.g. a flash, alternating patterns, etc) and measuring electrical brain waves over the occipital cortex. It provides a rough estimate of the function of the entire afferent visual pathway. An abnormal VEP does not aide in localizing pathology to any particular portion of the visual pathway (hence why answer A is incorrect). VEPs have very poor specificity. If a patient with vague neurological complaints shows no signs of multiple sclerosis (MS) on imaging, then a VEP to screen for MS is only going to complicate the clinical picture. With no prior objective findings to indicate an optic neuritis and no suspicious white matter changes on MRI, a VEP is not indicated in the scenario in answer B. A normal VEP can be useful to prove good vision in a patient suspected of functional vision loss, but the test does require good cooperation (especially a pattern-reversal VEP which provides the best assessment of visual acuity). An uncooperative patient will likely blink or defocus purposefully which will falsely reduce the pattern waveform and underestimate the function of the visual pathway. VEP's are an excellent tool for estimating visual function in patients unable to communicate such as young pre-verbal children or cognitively challenged patients. Again, however, pattern-reversal VEP's are the best test for estimating an actual visual acuity and require decent cooperation. Which of the following diseases is associated with a known auto-antibody that can be tested for to aid in diagnosis? A.cancer associated retinopathy (CAR) B.bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation (BDUMP) C.dominant optic atrophy (DOA) D.Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the tests that can aide in diagnosis of rare diseases (especially when they are fairly specific). CAR is associated with an auto-antibody to a 23 kd retinal photoreceptor protein called recoverin which functions in calcium binding. It is believed that there is a similar antigen located on certain carcinomas which the body rarely attacks with an antibody (anti- recoverin antibody). The “anti-recoverin antibody” then cross reacts with recoverin in the retina resulting in retinal destruction. Of note, melanoma associated retinopathy (MAR) has recently been found in some cases to be associated with auto-antibodies to the TRPM1 cation channel located on bipolar cells.1 This may become very helpful diagnostically in evaluation of possible MAR and may show up on future standardized tests. In the past MAR had been loosely associated with anti-transducin antibodies though the role and pathogenicity of these antibodies were not clear.2 DOA has an associated genetic mutation of the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3 in approximately 50-70% of families with clinical dominant optic atrophy. Vision loss in LHON is due to mitochondrial dysfunction. One of three pathogenic mitochondrial DNA point mutations at the 11778, 3460, and 14484 positions account for over 90% of LHON cases. BDUMP is a rare paraneoplastic melanocytic proliferation of choroidal melanocytes. For now, BDUMP remains a clinical diagnosis although there has been recently reported a BDUMP inducing protein that can tested for in a research lab setting termed "cultured melanocyte elongation and proliferation (CMEP) factor.3 There is no commercially available antibody test for the diagnosis of BDUMP (as of 02/2018). 1Dhingra A et al. Autoantibodies in melanoma-associated retinopathy target TRPM1 cation channels of retinal ON bipolar cells. J Neurosci. 2011;31:3962-7. 2 Potter MJ et al. Autoantibodies to transducin in a patient with melanoma-associated retinopathy. Am J Ophthalmol. 2002 Jul;134(1):128-30. 3 Joyce C et al. Early Diagnosis and Successful Treatment of Paraneoplastic Melanocytic Proliferation. Br J Ophthalmol. 2015 Jul:99(7):943-8. A macular sparing homonymous hemianopia is specific to a lesion in WHICH cerebral lobe and most likely caused by stroke of WHICH artery? A.occipital; posterior cerebral B.occipital; middle cerebral C.parietal; posterior cerebral D.parietal; middle cerebral High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Because of the anatomy and vascular supply of the optic pathways, only lesions of the occipital lobe can produce a macular sparing homonymous hemianopia. There are two vascular supplies to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the majority of the primary visual cortex responsible for the contralateral visual hemifield. The middle cerebral artery supplies the very posterior tip of the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe responsible for the contralateral macular portion of the hemifield. Therefore, a stroke of the PCA affecting the occipital lobe is the most likely cause of a macular- sparing homonymous hemianopia. 70-year old monocular patient with subtle dry macular degeneration and a history of normal tension glaucoma presents with decreased central vision. Which of the following is a method to help distinguish whether her visual deficit is due to optic nerve disease or macular disease? A.Humphrey visual field (HVF) B.Goldmann visual field (GVF) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Photostress recovery time High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Both macular degeneration and normal tension glaucoma can give rise to central / paracentral visual field deficits so neither a HVF or a GVF would be the best test to distinguish between these two entities. A potential acuity meter (PAM) projects a Snellen chart through hazy media on to the retina as a means to test a patient's potential vision (assessing the patient's visual function from the macula to the occipital cortex). A PAM test is one option for testing visual potential in cataract patients preoperatively. The photostress recovery time is a "poor man's electroretinogram." A photorecovery test begins with measuring the patient's best corrected visual acuity. Then a bright light is shined into the patient's eye for 10 seconds through undilated pupils. When the light is removed, the patient is asked to read the same BCVA line (or one line larger). The time required before the patient can read the BCVA line (or one line larger) is called the photostress recovery time. A normal photostress recovery time varies depending on which source you look at: some sources suggest less than 27 seconds others state less than 45-60 seconds. Recovery times > 90 seconds clearly indicate a significant maculopathy. This test is a good "old school" test to distinguish optic nerve disease from macular disease and can be helpful in certain patients. Please save us all your hateful comments about how lame photostress recovery time testing is in the clinical setting and just know that it is a testable topic on standardized exams as one way to distinguish a photoreceptor dysfunction-related maculopathy from an optic neuropathy. Which of the following is NOT TRUE of optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH)? A.there is a strong correlation between optic disc size and visual acuity B.unilateral or bilateral ONH can be associated with midline brain defects C.unilateral or bilateral ONH can be associated with endocrine dysfunction D.the superior segmental hypoplasia variant is associated with maternal diabetes during pregnancy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: While counterintuitive, optic disc size and visual acuity are not well-correlated in ONH. Very small optic discs may retain normal visual acuity while seemingly less hypoplastic nerves have markedly diminished vision. Visual acuity can range from 20/20 to NLP in ONH. It is very important that all children with unilateral or bilateral ONH undergo MRI and endocrine testing. ONH is associated with midline brain structural abnormalities and pituitary hormone imbalance as part of "de Morsier syndrome" (aka septo-optic dysplasia). Endocrine dysfunction due to pituitary hormone imbalance can occur in patients with monocular ONH and in ONH cases with no apparent midline brain abnormalities on MRI. For that reason, all patients with ONH should undergo an MRI and endocrine consultation. Brain abnormalities associated with ONH include hypoplasia or absence of the corpus callosum, the pituitary gland, and the septum pellucidum. A variant of ONH, involving only the superior aspect of the optic nerve and causing an inferior visual field defect, is highly associated with maternal diabetes during pregnancy. Of note, skull base bony defects may lead to basal encephaloceles that can mimic nasal polyps on exam. While optic nerve hypoplasia and morning glory disc anomaly are not the same entity, BOTH are associated with encephaloceles (high yield topic for some odd reason).

question: A macular sparing homonymous hemianopia is specific to a lesion in WHICH cerebral lobe and most likely caused by stroke of WHICH artery?
explanation: Because of the anatomy and vascular supply of the optic pathways, only lesions of the occipital lobe can produce a macular sparing homonymous hemianopia. There are two vascular supplies to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the majority of the primary visual cortex responsible for the contralateral visual hemifield. The middle cerebral artery supplies the very posterior tip of the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe responsible for the contralateral macular portion of the hemifield. Therefore, a stroke of the PCA affecting the occipital lobe is the most likely cause of a macular- sparing homonymous hemianopia. 70-year old monocular patient with subtle dry macular degeneration and a history of normal tension glaucoma presents with decreased central vision. Which of the following is a method to help distinguish whether her visual deficit is due to optic nerve disease or macular disease? A.Humphrey visual field (HVF) B.Goldmann visual field (GVF) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Photostress recovery time High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Both macular degeneration and normal tension glaucoma can give rise to central / paracentral visual field deficits so neither a HVF or a GVF would be the best test to distinguish between these two entities. A normal photostress recovery time varies depending on which source you look at: some sources suggest less than 27 seconds others state less than 45-60 seconds. question: Which of the pictured optic nerves (A-D) would you expect to see on fundus exam of the left eye?
explanation: The question describes a classic presentation of non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The risk factors for NAION include vasculopathic risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes , hypercholesterolemia, and smoking. Virtually all patients with NAION also have crowded optic nerves (photo A) with small cup-to-disc (C:D) ratios. It is difficult to know what a patient's C:D ratio is once disc swelling has set in but usually optic nerve appearance is symmetric and examination of the contralateral optic nerve is helpful. If the contralateral optic nerve has a C:D larger than 0.3 then the diagnosis of NAION should be reconsidered carefully. It would be important to reconsider occult arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis along with other causes of optic neuropathy in that scenario. Of the pictures shown, image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio ("disc at risk"). Image B shows a hypoplastic optic nerve head with a classic "double ring sign." Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o'clock. Image D shows mild to moderate temporal pallor. A patient has a normally reactive pupil in the right eye and a chronically-dilated and unreactive pupil in the left eye from a prior trauma. What findings would prove an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the left eye? A.it is only possible to check for an APD in the right eye B.it is impossible to check for an APD in either eye C.with the swinging flashlight test, the clinician should observe the right eye for dilation after swinging the light to the left eye D.with the swinging flashlight test, the clinician should observe the right eye for constriction after swinging the light to the left eye. High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: It is still possible to check for an APD when one eye has abnormal efferent function of the iris for whatever reason (dilating drops, prior trauma, Adies pupil, CN 3 palsy, etc). The proper method in these cases is to carefully observe the normally reactive iris/pupil while swinging the light from the normal pupil to the abnormal pupil. If there is no APD in the clinical scenario described in this question, then the right pupil will either remain the same size or constrict slightly upon swinging the flashlight from the right to the left eye. If an APD is present in the left eye, then the right pupil should dilate upon swinging the light from the right eye to the left eye. This method is often called checking for an APD "by reverse" although some neuro-ophthalmologists reject this terminology and feel it is a misnomer. A patient with a short attention span who is taking a 24-2 Humphrey visual field (HVF) performs poorly on the test because he repeatedly signals when a stimulus is presented in the expected physiologic location of his blind spot. What reliability parameter would most directly be affected by this poor performance? A.high false-positive response rate B.high false-negative response rate C.high fixation losses D.highly negative mean deviation High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The three reliability parameters on a HVF are the rate of false positive responses, false negative responses, and fixation losses. False positive responses occur when a patient is "trigger happy" and signals when he/she should not be able to see the stimulus (based on other stimulus testing in the same visual field region). False negative responses occur when a patient fails to signal when he or she should (again based on other stimulus testing in the same visual field region). Fixation losses occur when the patient is not fixated on the fixation light and he/she erroneously signals when a stimulus is presented in the area of his/her physiologic blind spot. Mean deviation (MD) is a global index of retinal sensitivity (the mean of all values in a total deviation plot). While the MD may be affected by reliability, it is not itself a reliability parameter.

question: What is the name of this constellation of findings and what is the most likely etiology in this case (given the visual field findings)?

options.A: Pseudo Foster Kennedy syndrome; sequential non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)
options.B: Pseudo Foster Kennedy syndrome; frontal lobe intracranial mass
options.C: Foster Kennedy syndrome; frontal lobe intracranial mass
options.D: Foster Kennedy syndrome; sequential non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)

explanation: Both Pseudo Foster Kennedy syndrome (PFK) and Foster Kennedy (FK) syndrome demonstrate one swollen optic nerve and one atrophic optic nerve on examination. It is important to distinguish the two, however, because they have vastly different causes. PFK is much more common than FK and is due to sequential non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). In PFK, the atrophic optic nerve suffered an NAION event at least 6-8 weeks prior to presentation (to allow time for development of optic nerve pallor) and the swollen optic nerve suffers from an acute NAION. In this setting both nerves should show visual field changes consistent with NAION (e.g. altitudinal defect, arcuate defect, etc). In contrast, FK is due to an intracranial mass (classically due to a slow growing frontal lobe meningioma) which caused a unilateral compressive optic neuropathy. Over time, the mass grows large enough to obstruct CSF outflow. There is increased intracranial pressure (ICP) resulting in papilledema. Because an atrophic optic nerve does not swell in response to increased ICP, only one nerve demonstrates swelling. In FK, therefore, the eye with the atrophic optic nerve will demonstrate variable visual field defects (any type is possible) from a compressive optic neuropathy, but the visual field in the eye with papilledema will show only enlargement of the blind spot. In conclusion, the key to distinguishing PFK and FK clinically is the type of visual field defect in the eye with disc edema; FK will show only an enlarged blind spot and PFK will show a visual field defect consistent with NAION (for testing purposes you will likely be shown an altitudinal defect). For the harsh critics out there who will point out that this whole distinction between FK and PFK doesn't matter in this clinical vignette because the MRI will reveal the cause, just remember that standardized tests don't always simulate real clinical practice. Distinguishing FK from PFK is a highly testable topic and forces the examinee to understand the difference between papilledema related visual field defects and NAION related visual field defects. A 70-year-old male comes in with a complaint that his vision is "terrible" in both eyes and getting worse over the last few years. During the history his wife quickly chimes in that he often "doesn?t see things right in front of him" and has trouble telling time on a clock face. He had a recent MRI of the brain for these symptoms which showed only mild generalized atrophy of the brain appropriate for his age. On examination he has 20/25 vision in both eyes. His pupils, motility, alignment, intraocular pressures, slit lamp exam and dilated fundus exam is normal. His ocular examination is essentially normal except that he missed 9/9 color plates in both eyes including the two color plates demonstrated above. When you point to the individual colors within the color plates, the patient seems to be able to identify colors accurately. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case? A.Posterior cortical atrophy B.Cone degeneration C.Occipital lobe seizures D.Occult giant cell arteritis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior cortical atrophy (PCA) is a slowly progressive senile degeneration that predominately affects the parietal and occipital lobes early in the disease course resulting in difficulty with visuospatial tasks and visual processing. Histopathology of PCA brain specimens usually shows an Alzheimer's type of degeneration leading to the term "visual variant of Alzheimer's disease" that is sometimes used as a synonym of PCA. Patients with PCA often present with vague visual complaints similar to this patient. PCA is frequently misdiagnosed because the complaints are vague, the ocular examination is structurally normal, and Snellen visual acuity may remain normal in the early stages of the disease. Over time the degeneration usually generalizes and results in memory deficits and cognitive decline similar to standard Alzheimer's disease. Neuro-imaging studies such as CT and MRI may show a relative atrophy in the parieto-occipital region, may show only diffuse atrophy, or may be normal. PCA can demonstrate a variety of visual deficits although the most common presentation is Balint syndrome (BS). BS is due to bilateral parieto-occipital dysfunction. The classic BS triad includes optic ataxia, acquired ocular motor apraxia, and simultanagnosia although most cases of Balint syndrome do not clearly demonstrate all three findings. Optic ataxia is essentially poor hand-eye coordination caused by a disconnect between vision and motor functions. There are many other causes of poor hand-eye coordination so this is not that helpful in making a diagnosis of Balint syndrome. Ocular apraxia is difficulty initiating saccades. Simultanagnosia is the most prevalent component of the Balint syndrome triad and is also the most useful sign to look for on examination. It is the failure to understand the entire meaning of a picture despite retaining the ability to recognize isolated objects within the picture. In other words, patients with simultanagnosia cannot "see the forest through the trees." Simultanagnosia is often tested for by using the "cookie theft picture" from the NIH stroke scale. The picture has a complex scene; the examiner asks the patient to describe what is occurring in the picture. A patient with simultanagnosia may describe one item in the picture but will be unable to provide a complete interpretation of the scene. Similarly, Ishihara plates are actually complex images. A patient with simultanagnosia will have intact color vision but will be unable to identify the number within the pattern. Inability to identify color plates in an elderly patient should raise suspicion for PCA. Above are optic nerve images from a patient who presents with headaches and blurred vision. Which of the following statements is true regarding the punctate bright areas present diffusely on the optic nerve heads (and indicated by the white arrow)? A.They are always calcified B.They are always visible on computed tomography (CT) scans thorough the optic nerve C.They are a common cause of pseudopapilledema D.They are indicative of chronic papilledema High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: These optic nerve photos were taken from a patient with chronic papilledema for many years. The punctate bright areas are termed “pseudodrusen” and are indicative of chronic papilledema. These spots are actually believed to be exudates from extruded axoplasm of retinal ganglion cells. If you compare side-by-side with true optic nerve head drusen you will notice that pseudodrusen are generally smaller in comparison. Also, pseudodrusen are seen in optic nerves with other findings of true optic disc swelling whereas optic nerve head drusen generally are a cause of “pseudopapilledema.” Of course, a few very rare patients could have optic nerve head drusen AND papilledema in which case one would have to look at the morphology of the bright lesions to know if they are pseudodrusen or real drusen. Aside from pseudodrusen, these optic nerve demonstrate other findings of papilledema including hyperemia of the optic nerve head. Hyperemia is one of the earliest findings of papilledema and persists until optic nerve atrophy occurs. In some patients with chronic papilledema and severe loss of retinal ganglion cells axons, the hyperemia can be replaced by pallor and “gliosis.” Other findings of true papilledema seen on this photo (reference explanation image below) are faint Paton lines indicated by the white arrow. These are concentric chorioretinal folds that eminate off a swollen optic nerve. Papilledema can cause radial chorioretinal folds / lines in the macula but these don't technically go by the name "Paton lines." On the photos there are also areas of clear vessel obscuration as the blood vessels cross the margin of the optic nerve. Because the blood vessels run deep to the nerve fiber layer (NFL), swelling of the NFL from true disc edema causes a blurring of the vessel appearance on the surface of the optic nerve head and at its margin. Most cases of pseudopapilledema (myelinated nerve fiber layer being a noteworthy exception) do NOT cause obscuration of the vessels. While there are numerous areas of vessel obscuration on these optic nerves, the yellow arrow points to one good example. The green arrow highlights an optociliary shunt vessel which serves as a collateral from the retinal venous drainage to the choroidal venous drainage. In chronic papilledema (like other causes of optociliary shunt vessels), there is a chronic obstruction to drainage of the central retinal vein leading to engorgement of venous collaterals that allow drainage of retinal venous blood into the choroidal venous circulation. There are more obvious examples of optociliary shunt vessels than that seen in this picture but this subtle finding is one more important clue to the chronicity of papilledema in this patient. For clarification of answer choices A-C which make reference to true optic nerve head drusen, optic nerve head drusen are NOT always calcified. CT can be helpful for showing calcified drusen (as can B-scan) but given the radiation exposure, expense, and requirement for just the right slices through the optic nerve head, CT is not first line for the diagnosis of optic nerve head drusen. Optic nerve head drusen are a very common cause of pseudopapilledema.

question: Above are optic nerve images from a patient who presents with headaches and blurred vision. Which of the following statements is true regarding the punctate bright areas present diffusely on the optic nerve heads (and indicated by the white arrow)?

options.B: They are always visible on computed tomography (CT) scans thorough the optic nerve
options.C: They are a common cause of pseudopapilledema
options.D: They are indicative of chronic papilledema

explanation: These optic nerve photos were taken from a patient with chronic papilledema for many years. The punctate bright areas are termed “pseudodrusen” and are indicative of chronic papilledema. These spots are actually believed to be exudates from extruded axoplasm of retinal ganglion cells. If you compare side-by-side with true optic nerve head drusen you will notice that pseudodrusen are generally smaller in comparison. Also, pseudodrusen are seen in optic nerves with other findings of true optic disc swelling whereas optic nerve head drusen generally are a cause of “pseudopapilledema.” Of course, a few very rare patients could have optic nerve head drusen AND papilledema in which case one would have to look at the morphology of the bright lesions to know if they are pseudodrusen or real drusen. Aside from pseudodrusen, these optic nerve demonstrate other findings of papilledema including hyperemia of the optic nerve head. Hyperemia is one of the earliest findings of papilledema and persists until optic nerve atrophy occurs. In some patients with chronic papilledema and severe loss of retinal ganglion cells axons, the hyperemia can be replaced by pallor and “gliosis.” Other findings of true papilledema seen on this photo (reference explanation image below) are faint Paton lines indicated by the white arrow. These are concentric chorioretinal folds that eminate off a swollen optic nerve. Papilledema can cause radial chorioretinal folds / lines in the macula but these don't technically go by the name "Paton lines." On the photos there are also areas of clear vessel obscuration as the blood vessels cross the margin of the optic nerve. Because the blood vessels run deep to the nerve fiber layer (NFL), swelling of the NFL from true disc edema causes a blurring of the vessel appearance on the surface of the optic nerve head and at its margin. Most cases of pseudopapilledema (myelinated nerve fiber layer being a noteworthy exception) do NOT cause obscuration of the vessels. While there are numerous areas of vessel obscuration on these optic nerves, the yellow arrow points to one good example. The green arrow highlights an optociliary shunt vessel which serves as a collateral from the retinal venous drainage to the choroidal venous drainage. In chronic papilledema (like other causes of optociliary shunt vessels), there is a chronic obstruction to drainage of the central retinal vein leading to engorgement of venous collaterals that allow drainage of retinal venous blood into the choroidal venous circulation. There are more obvious examples of optociliary shunt vessels than that seen in this picture but this subtle finding is one more important clue to the chronicity of papilledema in this patient. For clarification of answer choices A-C which make reference to true optic nerve head drusen, optic nerve head drusen are NOT always calcified. CT can be helpful for showing calcified drusen (as can B-scan) but given the radiation exposure, expense, and requirement for just the right slices through the optic nerve head, CT is not first line for the diagnosis of optic nerve head drusen. Optic nerve head drusen are a very common cause of pseudopapilledema.

question: A 60-year old male with NLP vision in both eyes from bilateral occipital lobe strokes still at times seems to be able to see large targets when they are moving across his visual field. Assuming you find this to be true on examination (and the patient isn't crazy), what is the name for this finding?
explanation: The Riddoch phenomenon is the ability to see moving targets for some patients with cortical blindness who are unable to see any stationary targets. While the underlying explanation for this rare and strange phenomenon is debated, some believe this reflects the fact that cells in the visual system respond better to moving objects compared to stationary ones. Here is a video of a patient with the syndrome: Riddoch phenomenon. Anton syndrome is the rather bizarre denial of blindness usually found in patients with cortical blindness. Pulfrich phenomenon is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. Usually however, it is described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) occurs when patients with severe bilateral visual loss of any type (often macular degeneration, glaucoma, or cortical blindness) see formed and unformed visual hallucinations. A patient with an absolute superior altitudinal defect from non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy has no response to the V4e stimulus on Goldmann perimetry in the region of the defect. What is the area in mm2 of this light stimulus? A.64 mm2 B.32 mm2 C.16 mm2 D.4 mm2 High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: The target size in Goldmann perimetry is represented by a Roman numeral (0-V). The smallest target size is 0 which equals 1/16 mm2. Every successive Roman numeral has an area 4 times the previous such that target size I = 1/4 mm2, II = 1 mm2, III = 4 mm2, IV = 16 mm2, and V = 64 mm2. An absolute scotoma is in theory a scotoma so dense that the corresponding area of retina has zero retinal sensitivity to light. In practice, an absolute scotoma is confirmed on Goldmann perimetry by testing with the brightest and largest target size (V4e). The Arabic numeral represents the intensity of the stimulus presented with 1 being the least intense and 4 being the most intense. The lowercase letter represents the filter used to dim the light with "a" being the darkest (or most dense filter) and "e" being the lightest filter. All of the following are true of posterior ischemic optic neuropathy EXCEPT: A.Disc edema is usually present B.It is associated with hypotension and anemia C.It can be associated with giant cell arteritis D.Is most commonly seen following coronary artery bypass and spine surgery High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely, PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV-related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Optic pallor typically begins to appear six to eight weeks after the PION event. Which mitochondrial DNA point mutation is the most common pathogenic mutation in Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)? A.11778 B.14484 C.3460 D.5780 High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The point mutations 11778, 14484, and 3460 account for over 90% of LHON. Therefore, these are the mutations most commonly tested for when a LHON screening blood test is sent off. How long after initiating steroid treatment can a temporal artery biopsy be delayed in cases of giant cell arteritis (GCA) before compromising the diagnostic yield? A.6 hours B.24 hours C.1-3 days D.1-2 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: In suspected cases of GCA, steroid therapy should be initiated immediately. The clinician should NEVER wait for a biopsy before initiating treatment if the patient is believed to have GCA. A patient with a recent right parietal lobe cerebrovascular accident (CVA) has full confrontation fields in both eyes when assessed with finger counting in one visual field quadrant of one eye at a time. However, when multiple targets are presented to the same eye simultaneously in different hemifields, the patient exhibits a left homonymous hemianopia. What is the term for this phenomenon? A.gaze preference B.visual allesthesia C.the Pulfrich phenomenon D.extinction High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: A form of neglect involving the visual field, extinction describes the inability to see a stimulus in one hemifield of an eye only when a target is simultaneously presented in both hemifields of that eye. When a stimulus is tested by itself in the hemifield exhibiting extinction, the stimulus is seen. Extinction is usually associated with parietal lobe lesions and the phenomena would be exhibited in the contralateral hemifield of both eyes. Gaze preference is the tendency to look with both eyes in a certain direction although the patient retains the ability to look in other directions if they choose (distinguishing gaze preference from gaze palsy). Visual allesthesia is when patients see their environment as rotated or inverted and usually occurs with lesions in the lateral medullary region or the occipitoparietal region of the brain. Pulfrich phenomena is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. It is usually described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Which of the following can be a sign of a pituitary mass? A.Down-beat nystagmus B.Binasal visual field defects C.Hemifield slide D.Pre-fixational blindness High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: The following may be seen in pituitary tumours: • Chiasmatic post fixational blindness is related to the loss of the temporal field bilaterally resulting in a blind area beyond fixation. During close work (convergence), an object placed just beyond fixation (therefore in temporal field) may disappear • Hemifield slide is related to disruption of ocular fusion and decompensation of a previous phoria. If the eyes intermittently converge, there is a central strip that is not seen. If the eyes have an intermittent exotropia, there will be overlap of the central vertical meridian. • See-saw nystagmus is a type of pendular nystagmus where a half cycle consists of the elevation and intorsion of one eye, concurrently with the depression and extortion of the fellow eye. • Bitemporal visual field defect Functioning Tumours • Acromegaly/gigantism, cushings, hyperprolactinaemia (impotence, galactorrhoea). • Treat prolactin secreting with cabergoline or bromocriptine, growth hormone secreting with octreotide. Destructive lesions • Hypopituitarism with low FSH/LH (low libido, amenorrhoea), hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism with collapse. • Hypothalamic/posterior pituitary involvement may cause diabetes insipidus (reduced ADH, polydipsia, polyuria). Which of the following is FALSE regarding the morning glory disc (MGD) anomaly? A.it is more common in males B.it is usually unilateral C.affected eyes typically have poor visual acuity (< 20/200) D.serous retinal detachments occur in approximately 30% of affected eyes High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Morning glory disc (MGD) anomalies are congenital, generally unilateral, and more common in females. They often result in poor vision and an afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye. The branch retinal vessels typically emanate in a radial fashion from the far periphery of the excavated, staphylomatous nerve head. There are three associations with MGD that clinicians should be aware of and are frequently tested: (1) Similar to optic nerve head pits, serous retinal detachments frequently occur in eyes with MGD. (2) Occult, transsphenoidal basal encephaloceles may be present in patients with MGD. Similar to basal encephaloceles associated with optic nerve hypoplasia, these can mimic nasal polyps on exam. (3) Moyamoya disease. This is a chronic progressive cerebrovascular disease characterized by bilateral stenosis or occlusion of the arteries around the Circle of Willis. The clinical consequences include TIAs, strokes, and epilepsy. Because of the latter two associations, a MRI/MRA of the brain should be obtained in all patients with MGD. Assuming all unmentioned exam findings are normal, which of the following patients would be least likely to demonstrate a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) on exam? A.a 24-year old with count fingers vision OD and near total cupping of the optic nerve OD following a trauma to the right eye 5 years ago. B.a 75-year old with right temporal headaches, jaw claudication, sudden vision loss in the right eye to light perception, and a pale swollen optic nerve OD. C.a 50-year old who awoke from a complicated 12-hour spine surgery with light perception vision in both eyes. Both optic nerves and the MRI of the brain/orbits are normal one day after surgery. A spinning OKN drum fails to elicit any nystagmus from either eye. D.a 10-year old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1 and an optic glioma of the right optic nerve with 20/100 vision OD and 20/20 vision OS. The right optic nerve shows pallor but the left is normal. High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: A RAPD measures the function of the afferent pupillary light reflex on one side compared to the other (referred to as a "relative" afferent pupillary defect for that reason although many people simply omit the "relative"). Vision often (though not always) correlates with the presence of an APD. All the scenarios above involve significant damage to the optic nerve in question but only scenario 3 (a case of posterior ischemic optic neuropathy) is bilateral. Since both optic nerves are severely affected, it is not surprising that there is no relative difference in function of the optic nerves. Of note, one would expect poor pupillary responses in both eyes in the patient described in answer choice C. A 22-year-old male presents as a referral from his optometrist for asymptomatic inferior visual field defects in both eyes found on a routine eye exam. Your exam shows normal visual acuity, color vision, and pupil function in both eyes. A color photograph of his right optic nerve appearance and corresponding right eye automated Humphrey visual field 30-2 are shown above. The left optic nerve and left eye visual field appear nearly identical. The remainder of the dilated fundus exam is unremarkable in both eyes. Which of the following is commonly associated with this diagnosis? A.Maternal diabetes B.High intraocular pressures C.Nystagmus D.Absence of the septum pellucidum High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This is a classic presentation of segmental optic nerve hypoplasia. It is a congenital, non- progressive condition marked by segmental maldevelopment of the optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer. In the vast majority of cases only the superior half of the optic disc is hypoplastic leading to another common term for this entity- “topless optic disc syndrome.” Patients often present with little or no recognition of severe, lifelong bilateral inferior visual field defects that spare fixation. The papillomacular bundle arising from the temporal aspect of the optic nerve is spared resulting in normal visual acuity and color vision. Segmental optic nerve hypoplasia is often symmetric thus pupil testing is typically normal without an afferent pupillary defect. This diagnosis is commonly associated with maternal diabetes during pregnancy and is thought to reflect a teratogenic effect of high blood sugars. This has been reported in one study to occur in about 8% of type 1 diabetic mothers (although this author feels that is probably an overestimate given the relative rarity of the diagnosis in clinical practice). Unlike septo-optic dysplasia (SOD), or De Morsier syndrome, segmental optic nerve hypoplasia is typically isolated without other associated endocrine or neurologic sequelae. SOD, on the other hand, is a congenital disease characterized by midline brain developmental abnormalities (e.g. absence of the septum pellucidum), hypopituitarism, and unilateral or bilateral “non-segmental” optic nerve hypoplasia. Visual acuity can range from near normal to severely impaired in SOD. High intraocular pressures would be expected in congenital glaucoma and juvenile glaucoma but the optic nerve has a vastly different appearance. Because visual acuity is typically normal in patients with segmental optic nerve hypoplasia, nystagmus is not associated with segmental optic nerve hypoplasia like it is with SOD associated optic nerve hypoplasia. Below the bright green brackets are used to illustrate the top half versus the bottom half of the neuro-retinal rim. This highlights a markedly abnormal asymmetry with relative hypoplasia of the superior half of the optic nerve compared to the inferior.

question: Which of the following is FALSE regarding the morning glory disc (MGD) anomaly?

question: In a patient with diagnosed optic neuritis, which optic nerve description in the affected eye correlates to the lowest risk of multiple sclerosis (MS) development in the future?

options.D: severe disc edema with peripapillary hemorrhages

explanation: This seems counterintuitive but the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial found severe optic disc edema with peripapillary retinal hemorrhages to be inversely related to the risk of MS development. In fact, among patients with peripapillary hemorrhages and a normal brain MRI, no patients developed MS at the 10 year mark. That is a stark contrast compared to all patients with optic neuritis and a normal brain MRI which had about a 20% chance of MS development by 10 years. Patients with a clinical presentation of optic neuritis but who have massive disc edema and hemorrhages usually have other etiologies for their optic nerve dysfunction such as infectious or autoimmune inflammatory conditions (e.g. sarcoidosis, lupus associated optic neuritis, etc) rather than demyelination of the optic nerve associated with MS. This form of optic neuritis with massive disc edema and hemorrhages is often referred to "atypical optic neuritis" as opposed to "idiopathic demyelinating optic neuritis." What is the visual field defect classically seen early in the course of a slowly-progressive toxic optic neuropathy or nutritional optic neuropathy? A.Cecocentral and/or central defects B.Global depression C.Arcuate defect D.Ring scotoma High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Cecocentral and/or central defects are classically seen in early toxic optic neuropathy and nutritional optic neuropathy. Global depression can occur in severe end-stage toxic optic neuropathy, but is not the most likely defect early in the disease course of slowly progressive toxic optic neuropathies. Acute toxic optic neuropathies from methanol or ethylene glycol may present more commonly with global depression. Arcuate defects are typically seen in nerve fiber bundle defects caused by glaucoma and optic nerve drusen. Ring scotomas are classic for retinitis pigmentosa, but could occur in acquired rod predominant degenerations such as vitamin A deficiency or melanoma associated retinopathy. Visual field defects respecting the vertical meridian and imitating a bitemporal hemianopia are not unusual in toxic neuropathy due to ethambutol. pituitary masses classically result in what combination of visual field defects? A.Central visual loss in one eye with a superotemporal deficit in the contralateral eye B.Bilateral mostly superotemporal deficits respecting the vertical midline but extending to a complete bitemporal hemianopia late in the disease course C.A bitemporal hemianopic type defect of the central 5-10 degrees only D.Bilateral mostly inferotemporal deficits respecting the vertical midline but extending to a complete bitemporal hemianopia late in the disease course High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Pituitary masses classically compress the middle portion of the inferior optic chiasm. The retinal ganglion cell axons first compromised by such compression would be the inferonasal fibers supplying the superotemporal visual fields in both eyes. With increasing compression, more fibers become involved and the deficits may progress to a complete hemianopia. Please see the image below to help you visualize how enlargement of the pituituary gland (red structure) first affects the inferior portion of the optic chiasm.

question: Occlusion of what blood vessel most likely led to this constellation of findings?
explanation: The MRI images provided above demonstrate a T2 hyperintense region in the left dorsal lateral region of the medulla. The diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) sequence shows hyperintensity in the same region indicating restricted diffusion. Together these findings support the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke of the left dorso-lateral medulla which is also known clinically as Wallenberg syndrome (WS). The medulla is full of important pathways including many that affect the eyes and eyelids. WS is classically characterized by a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral side of the body (due to impairment of the lateral spinothalamic tract) and ipsilateral side of the face (due to impairment of the spinal trigeminal tract). There is also ipsilateral Horner syndrome due to loss of ipsilateral descending sympathetic fibers. The sympathetic pathway involves a series of three orders of neurons and is quite complicated. It is important, however, to remember that the sympathetic fibers throughout their 3 neuron system NEVER decussate. Therefore a lesion affecting the sympathetic pathway will ALWAYS be ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome it causes. Damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle as it enters the medulla results in ipsilateral ataxia (of the limbs) and ipsilateral axial lateropulsion (falling to the same side of the lesion when walking). Damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the vestibular nuclei results in nystagmus. Other associated features include vertigo (from vestibular dysfunction), diplopia (from skew deviation), and uncontrollable hiccups (from vagal nerve dysfunction). The lateral medulla is usually served by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) so this would be the most commonly occluded vessel in cases of WS. In fact, another name for WS is posterior inferior cerebellar artery syndrome. A 25-year-old female just moved to the area and comes to you for a routine eye check. You find her best corrected vision to be 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS although she has no complaints regarding her vision. The fundus exam is completely normal in both eyes. She states that her left eye has "always been weaker" than her right. Which of the following would prompt you to further work up this patient's vision loss? A.a 3+ afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the left eye B.a 5 prism diopter microesotropia with a history of strabismus surgery as a child C.a refraction of -2.00 diopters OD and -6.00 diopters OS D.none of the findings above would prompt a more detailed work-up High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Long standing amblyopia can be difficult to recognize in an adult. Hopefully patients with amblyopia will give a history that one eye "never saw as well as the other." Often patients demonstrate on exam or volunteer a history of strabismus, anisometropia, patching, or some other childhood eye disorder which suggests amblyopia. Both a microesotropia following strabismus surgery and anisometropia are reassuring features in a patient with suspected amblyopia because they support the working diagnosis. Amblyopia can result in an APD but typically the vision and the degree of the APD will correlate. In other words, when amblyopia results in an APD there is typically severe vision loss and relatively mild APD. In this patient, the APD is much more pronounced then the vision loss and therefore the patient should have a more extensive work-up (starting with neuro-imaging of the brain and orbits: preferably an MRI). Amsler grid testing evaluates how many central degrees of the visual field? A.20 B.15 C.5 D.2.5 High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: The Amsler grid tests the central 20 degrees (i.e. 10 degrees on either side of fixation) and is often used at home by patients with macular degeneration to assess for any acute changes in vision in between office visits. Humphrey visual field testing can test the central 20 degrees (10-2 protocol), 48 x 54 degrees (vertical x horizontal) (24-2), or 60 degrees (30-2) depending on the study type chosen. Tangent screens are typically used to evaluate the central 30 degrees with the patient seated 1 meter in front of the screen, although the size of the testing field can be changed by moving the patient forward or backward. Goldman visual fields are used to evaluate the entire visual field (the machine can test up to 180 degrees horizontally which far outreaches the potential monocular visual field in humans). Lesions compressing the most anterior aspect of the optic chiasm at the crossroads of one optic nerve and the chiasm can result in what combination of visual field defects? A.Full field visual loss in one eye with a superotemporal deficit in the contralateral eye B.Symmetric bitemporal hemianopia of both entire temporal fields C.A bitemporal hemianopic type defect of the central 5-10 degrees only D.Bilateral mostly inferotemporal deficits respecting the vertical midline High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Diffuse visual field loss with decreased visual acuity and a contralateral deficit in the superotemporal field is referred to as a junctional scotoma and is accurately localized to the junction of the optic nerve and the chiasm. The ipsilateral optic nerve compromise results in diffuse optic nerve dysfunction / central scotoma and the contalateral visual field is compromised due to the anatomic structure known as Willbrand's knee. Inferonasal retinal ganglion cell axons (serving the superotemporal field) decussate in the optic chiasm as they track posteriorly. Before entering the contralateral optic tract, however, they loop anteriorly for a short segment (called Willbrand's knee) into the contralateral optic nerve. Because of this anatomy, an anterior optic chiasm or far posterior optic nerve lesion causes vision loss in both eyes in this very specific fashion. The existence of Willbrand's knee remains controversial in that anatomic studies have shown Willbrand's knee is an artifact of post-mortem tissue sectioning. Nevertheless, no one disputes the localizing value of a junctional scotoma regardless of whether the Willbrand's knee explanation is valid. A 19-year-old otherwise healthy male comes in with two weeks of decreased vision in the left eye that developed acutely over several days. His review of systems is otherwise normal including a lack of eye pain. On examination he has 20/200 best corrected vision in the left eye, a 1+ left afferent pupillary defect, and diminished color plates. The fundus exam is significant for the findings seen above. Is neuro-imaging required in these patients and what is the risk for development of multiple sclerosis (MS)? A.No neuro-imaging required; No risk of MS over general population B.Neuro-imaging required; No risk of MS over general population C.Neuro-imaging required; 20% risk of MS over general population D.Neuro-imaging required; 60% risk of MS over general population High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient's presentation is suggestive of an acute left optic neuropathy given his vision loss, decreased color vision, and left afferent pupillary defect. The fundus findings are classic for neuroretinitis showing a swollen left optic nerve along with prominent macular exudates forming a "macular star." The optic neuritis treatment trial showed that neuroretinitis is not a risk factor for MS development. While there have been cases of demyelinating optic neuritis with macular exudates reported in patients with MS, most clinicians would agree that neuro-imaging is not necessary in patients with neuroretinitis unless they have other worrisome neurological symptoms. Lab testing for specific etiologies can be helpful, however, and would include tests to rule out Bartonella henselae ("cat scratch fever"), syphilis, sarcoidosis, toxoplasmosis, and Lyme disease. If the blood work is unrevealing then the diagnosis is idiopathic neuroretinitis which has also been termed "Leber's idiopathic stellate neuroretinitis" in the past. One note, in the past some reputable sources listed the most common cause of neuroretinitis as "idiopathic" with Bartonella henselae being the most common "infectious cause" or "known cause" although the modern BCSC now states that Bartonella h. is the etiology in 2/3 (and therefore most) cases of neuroretinitis. The truth probably depends on what literature you are referencing and the fact that Bartonella testing is more accurate, more available, and more commonly performed today.

Inferonasal retinal ganglion cell axons (serving the superotemporal field) decussate in the optic chiasm as they track posteriorly. Before entering the contralateral optic tract, however, they loop anteriorly for a short segment (called Willbrand's knee) into the contralateral optic nerve. Because of this anatomy, an anterior optic chiasm or far posterior optic nerve lesion causes vision loss in both eyes in this very specific fashion. The existence of Willbrand's knee remains controversial in that anatomic studies have shown Willbrand's knee is an artifact of post-mortem tissue sectioning. A 19-year-old otherwise healthy male comes in with two weeks of decreased vision in the left eye that developed acutely over several days. His review of systems is otherwise normal including a lack of eye pain. On examination he has 20/200 best corrected vision in the left eye, a 1+ left afferent pupillary defect, and diminished color plates. The fundus exam is significant for the findings seen above. Is neuro-imaging required in these patients and what is the risk for development of multiple sclerosis (MS)? A.No neuro-imaging required; No risk of MS over general population B.Neuro-imaging required; No risk of MS over general population C.Neuro-imaging required; 20% risk of MS over general population D.Neuro-imaging required; 60% risk of MS over general population High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient's presentation is suggestive of an acute left optic neuropathy given his vision loss, decreased color vision, and left afferent pupillary defect. The fundus findings are classic for neuroretinitis showing a swollen left optic nerve along with prominent macular exudates forming a "macular star." The optic neuritis treatment trial showed that neuroretinitis is not a risk factor for MS development. While there have been cases of demyelinating optic neuritis with macular exudates reported in patients with MS, most clinicians would agree that neuro-imaging is not necessary in patients with neuroretinitis unless they have other worrisome neurological symptoms. Lab testing for specific etiologies can be helpful, however, and would include tests to rule out Bartonella henselae ("cat scratch fever"), syphilis, sarcoidosis, toxoplasmosis, and Lyme disease. If the blood work is unrevealing then the diagnosis is idiopathic neuroretinitis which has also been termed "Leber's idiopathic stellate neuroretinitis" in the past. One note, in the past some reputable sources listed the most common cause of neuroretinitis as "idiopathic" with Bartonella henselae being the most common "infectious cause" or "known cause" although the modern BCSC now states that Bartonella h. is the etiology in 2/3 (and therefore most) cases of neuroretinitis. The truth probably depends on what literature you are referencing and the fact that Bartonella testing is more accurate, more available, and more commonly performed today.

question: Amsler grid testing evaluates how many central degrees of the visual field?
explanation: The Amsler grid tests the central 20 degrees (i.e. 10 degrees on either side of fixation) and is often used at home by patients with macular degeneration to assess for any acute changes in vision in between office visits. Tangent screens are typically used to evaluate the central 30 degrees with the patient seated 1 meter in front of the screen, although the size of the testing field can be changed by moving the patient forward or backward. Goldman visual fields are used to evaluate the entire visual field (the machine can test up to 180 degrees horizontally which far outreaches the potential monocular visual field in humans).
