question: A 33-year-old woman is referred to your clinic by her primary care physician (PCP) for a history of "papilledema." The patient sought care from her PCP due to some new, mild headaches. Examination of her optic discs is seen in the photo above. Her PCP ordered a head CT scan which is also shown above. Which of the following is the most common visual abnormality associated with this patient's ocular disorder?
explanation: The disc photos shows a "lumpy bumpy" margin of both optic discs. This appearance may simulate optic disc swelling since the discs appear elevated by the nodules buried underneath. The corresponding CT scan shows a calcification at the optic nerve head of the right eye (i.e. bright white dot on the CT). These findings are consistent with optic disc drusen (ODD). ODD is one of several possible causes of "pseudopapilledema" -- i.e. conditions that simulate the optic disc swelling of papilledema. Unlike true papilledema, there is no hyperemia of the disc, no hemorrhages, no exudates, and no obscuration of the retinal blood vessels as they cross the margin in ODD. Visual field loss is present in 75-90% of cases of ODD with enlargement of the blind spot being the most frequent type. However, transient obscurations of vision can also occur in ODD (5-10% of cases) and is thought to be due to transient disc ischemia. Decreased central visual acuity is a harbinger of other pathology unrelated to ODD and should prompt a work-up for compressive lesions. Rarely, ODD is associated with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. A 65-year old male undergoes 4-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting complicated by bleeding with hypotension. He is resuscitated, however, and seems to recover well initially. When he awakes sufficiently to communicate, he denies any vision problems but nurses say he doesn't seem to see anything. On exam he reads the 20/20 line of the near card quickly with both eyes but gets every letter wrong (and doesn't even appear to be looking at the card when testing). Likewise he doesn't identify the correct number of fingers on finger count testing nor does he identify consistently when a light is shined in either eye. His pupil exam is seemingly normal and the remainder of his ocular exam is unremarkable. Neuro-imaging demonstrates bilateral occipital lobe strokes. "My vision is fine," the patient says. What is the name for this patient's odd behavior? A.Pulfrich phenomenon B.Anton syndrome C.Riddoch phenomenon D.Charles Bonnet syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Anton syndrome is the rather bizarre denial of blindness usually found in patients with cortical blindness. Cortical blindness is blindness due to total bilateral impairment of the retrochiasmal optic pathway. While this could be due to bilateral lesions anywhere posterior to the chiasm, the reality is that bilateral temporal / parietal lobe lesions are often lethal or lead to so many other deficits that total visual loss is not recognized. Because lesions causing cortical blindness occur posterior to axons involved in the pupillary light reflex, patients with cortical blindness have normal pupillary exams with normal pupillary reactivity. Pulfrich phenomenon is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. Usually however, it is described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Riddoch phenomenon is the ability to see moving targets for some patients with cortical blindness who are unable to see any stationary targets. Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) occurs when patients with bilateral severe visual loss of any type (often macular degeneration, glaucoma, or cortical blindness) see formed and unformed visual hallucinations. They often describe seeing children or faces. Most patients with CBS have excellent insight into their hallucinations and know in the moment that the hallucinations are not real. A 14-month-old child presents to your clinic after his mom noted his eyes "shaking" since 3 months of age. He is small for his age and is significantly delayed in meeting all of his milestones. His mom fears that he does not see well. On examination you note fixation with intermittent following in both eyes. His pupils react to light and show no afferent pupillary defect. He has grossly full motility in both eyes and no strabismus. He does have prominent pendular nystagmus. The macula, vessels, and peripheral retina examination is normal in both eyes. His optic nerves are displayed above along with a recent MRI section demonstrating an important finding. What is the most common hormonal abnormality in these patients? A.Low thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) B.Low growth Hormone (GH) C.Low adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH) D.Low anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This child has septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) which is a congenital disease characterized by midline brain developmental abnormalities, hypopituitarism, and unilateral or bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia. Vision can range from near normal to severely impaired. Nystagmus is frequently present and develops around age 1-4 months when the pathways required for normal fixation typically mature. All children with optic nerve hypoplasia should have an MRI of the brain and an endocrine evaluation because anomalies in brain development and hypopituitarism are common. Growth hormone (GH) deficiency is the most common endocrinopathy found in approximately 70% of children with SOD while hypothyroidism (43%), adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency (27%), and diabetes insipidus (5%) are less common. A 65-year-old female (see photo above) with a history of a myocardial infarction, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia comes in with a complaint of ocular irritation and blurred vision for 2 months. Her best corrected acuity measures 20/25 in both the right and the left eye but under binocular conditions she says that her vision is blurred. Slit lamp exam shows conjunctival injection and papillary reaction superior to the cornea (not shown in the photo). What would be an appropriate next step? A.Reassurance B.Reassurance with artificial tears C.Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin testing D.Edrophonium testing High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The photo in this patient shows a vertical strabismus (with the right eye higher than the left) along with left upper more than right upper eyelid retraction. The patient should be diplopic but like many patients she has difficulty describing her symptoms. Instead of saying she has “double vision” she describes blurry vision under binocular conditions. The most common causes of double vision with vertical strabismus and eyelid retraction is thyroid associated ophthalmopathy. A second clue to this case is that the patient has slit lamp exam findings consistent with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) which has a strong association with thyroid dysfunction. Any patient with SLK should undergo testing for thyroid dysfunction (standard thyroid function tests and/or thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin). Reassurance would not be appropriate in this patient because the patient likely has an underlying thyroid disorder that should be treated. Myasthenia gravis can cause vertical strabismus and pseudo-retraction but has no association with SLK. While unlikely in this scenario, one could always consider adding a myasthenia work-up on to the patient’s evaluation (hence answer choice D) but given her history of a prior myocardial infarction, edrophonium testing could be dangerous. Edrophonium may result in arrhythmias such as bradycardia and is usually reserved for younger patients without a cardiac history. If myasthenia were being considered, a more appropriate, safe first test would be acetylcholine receptor antibodies. A 21-year-old young man presents to your clinic with acute, painless loss of vision in the right eye. His best corrected visual acuity is 20/100 and 20/20 in the right and left eyes respectively. There is an afferent pupillary defect (APD) OD. His exam is notable for hyperemia and elevation of the right optic disc but without leakage on fluorescein angiogram (FA). What is the most common visual field defect associated with this patient's likely disorder? A.altitudinal B.nasal step C.double arcuate D.cecocentral High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This young man presents with an optic neuropathy of the right eye with acutely decreased vision, an APD, and optic disc swelling. However, unlike inflammatory optic neuropathies (e.g. optic neuritis), there is no leakage on FA. His history and clinical findings are consistent with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). Other features of LHON include peripapillary telangiectasia, thickening of the peripapillary retina, and tortuosity of the medium-sized retinal arterioles. The most common visual field defect is a cecocentral defect. As discussed elsewhere in this section, LHON is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, usually at position 11778. Therefore, only mothers are capable of transmitting this disease to their offspring. The fellow eye typically has subclinical visual field abnormalities at presentation that eventually progress to mirror the first eye over the ensuing weeks or months. There is no proven treatment of this optic neuropathy. However, avoidance of tobacco and excess alcohol is probably prudent to decrease oxidative demand. An otherwise-healthy 25-year old male is assaulted by "two dudes" while "minding his own business." He was struck on the left side of the face and suffered immediate vision loss in the left eye. On testing, his vision in the right eye is 20/20 and left eye is 20/150. He has brisk pupillary reflexes without an afferent pupillary defect (APD). There is mild swelling in the left frontal region but no periocular swelling. Ocular motility is full and visual fields are full to confrontation with finger counting in both eyes. The slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable in both eyes. The patient says he knows the "two dudes" and he is going to sue them. Why does this patient definitely not have traumatic optic neuropathy (TON)? A.His vision should be worse than 20/150 with TON B.His fundus exam did not show disc edema C.He did not demonstrate an APD D.His visual field was full to confrontation High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Traumatic optic neuropathy always presents with an APD in the affected eye (assuming the contralateral eye has normal optic nerve function). TON can have mild to severe impairment of visual acuity and visual fields. Usually the damage occurs in the retrobulbar portion of the optic nerve in the optic canal so there is no disc swelling visible on fundus exam. Which of the following is NOT associated with small optic disc drusen (ODD)? A.tuberous sclerosis (TS) B.retinitis pigmentosa (RP) C.pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) D.Caucasian race High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: There seems to be a higher rate of small ODD in patients with RP and PXE. The literature suggests that in RP patients the ODD are often extruded along the margin of the optic disc providing a "scalloped" appearance and making the ODD more visible on exam. ODD rarely affects non-Caucasians. TS is associated with "mulberry-like" retinal astrocytic hamartomas. When present on the optic nerve head, astrocytic hamartomas can be confused with ODD. For the OQ over achievers who wish to learn something not currently published in the BCSC, Alagille syndrome, or arteriohepatic dysplasia, which is a disorder of familial intrahepatic cholestasis, is also highly associated with optic nerve head drusen. These patients are known to exhibit posterior embryotoxon but also usually have optic nerve head drusen. According to the initial study of 20 patients with AS that described this association, 95% had ultrasound evidence of drusen in at least one eye and 80% had bilateral optic nerve head drusen. See link to pubmed abstract. ishihara pseudoisochromatic color plates were designed to screen for what type of color vision deficiency? A.red-green deficiency B.blue-yellow deficiency C.all color vision deficiencies D.Ishihara plates do not test color vision High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates only test red-green deficiencies, so in theory, Ishihara plates could miss mild dyschromatopsias not in the red-green spectrum. In reality, however, most pathology that result in color vision loss (optic neuropathies / maculopathies) have a significant red-green component. Lanthony tritan plates are used to screen for blue-yellow deficiency, but they are less commonly used compared to Ishihara plates. For a more thorough evaluation of color vision one can use the Farnsworth Panel D-15 test, the Lanthony desaturated 15-hue test, or the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue test. These more detailed tests all involve arranging colored discs or chips in order of hue and intensity. Due to the time involved to administer them, they are seldom if ever used as screening tests. Which of the following examination techniques can differentiate between supranuclear and non- supranuclear lesions? A.Saccades B.Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) C.Convergence D.Doll’s head manoeuvre High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Differentiating supranuclear from nuclear and infranuclear lesions can be done using the oculocephalic and vestibulo-ocular reflex testing. Oculocephalic (Doll's eyes) reflex The oculocephalic (Doll's eyes) reflex is performed by tilting the head forward 30 degrees and fixating a distant target. The head is then rotated in the direction opposite the gaze palsy. Gaze palsies caused by lesions of the cerebral cortex can typically be overcome by vestibulo-ocular testing. In prenuclear, nuclear, or infranuclear lesions, the reflex does not overcome the palsy. Vestibulo-ocular reflex testing The patient's head is tilted back 60 degrees and the external auditory meatus irrigated with either cool or warm water to stimulate the horizontal semicircular canal. When warm water is used, the fast phase is toward the stimulated ear. The mnemonic COWS (cool, opposite, warm, same) refers to the direction of the fast phase of the nystagmus. In comatose patients, no corrective (fast) phase occurs. A 40-year-old otherwise healthy African American female comes in complaining of 1 year of intermittent jumping vision and binocular diplopia with images oblique to one another. Between episodes her vision is fine. Each episodes last anywhere from a “split second” to “minutes” and episodes have become more frequently recently. The patient astutely notices that the episodes are sometimes triggered when she looks down or tilts her head to the left. Above is a video showing pertinent exam findings. What is the diagnosis in this case? ( video missing ) A.Cyclotorsional nystagmus B.Volitional nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Superior oblique myokymia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This is a classic case of superior oblique myokymia (SOM) characterized by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. SOM is almost always unilateral and in this patient is occurring in the left eye only. While some patients can recognize which eye is jumping often people are unable to describe the history in that detail. The differential diagnosis for jumping vision in one eye is very limited and almost always is caused by SOM although ocular neuromyotonia (often related to prior iatrogenic radiation exposure) would be another possibility. While the etiology of SOM is usually unknown, some cases of SOM demonstrate MRI findings of vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Other proposed theories for SOM include axonal regeneration following mild damage to the trochlear nerve (from any cause) leading to aberrant spontaneous discharges of the nerve. SOM usually causes a fine amplitude oscillatory contraction of the superior oblique muscle (as is seen in this video in the left eye). Observing the conjunctival vessels with the slit lamp will often allow the observer to clearly see small amplitude episodic incyclotorsional and infraduction movements of the affected eye. Patients experience this as monocular oscillopsia and binocular diplopia. Stressing the superior oblique muscle by head tilt towards the ipsilateral side or looking down can often trigger an event of SOM. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work- ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is typically horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. Pure cyclotorsional, or rotary, nystagmus is not a diagnosis but rather a finding that can occur due to many different etiologies. This would be expected to be bilateral and would not be worse looking down and with an ipsilateral head tilt. Square wave jerks are a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase typical of nystagmus and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or intersaccadic interval) and then a quick return to fixation. An occasional square wave jerk is physiologic but frequent square wave jerks (more than 9 per minute) raise concern for cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and progressive supranuclear palsy.

A.red-green deficiency B.blue-yellow deficiency C.all color vision deficiencies D.Ishihara plates do not test color vision High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates only test red-green deficiencies, so in theory, Ishihara plates could miss mild dyschromatopsias not in the red-green spectrum. Which of the following examination techniques can differentiate between supranuclear and non- supranuclear lesions? A.Saccades B.Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) C.Convergence D.Doll’s head manoeuvre High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Differentiating supranuclear from nuclear and infranuclear lesions can be done using the oculocephalic and vestibulo-ocular reflex testing. Oculocephalic (Doll's eyes) reflex The oculocephalic (Doll's eyes) reflex is performed by tilting the head forward 30 degrees and fixating a distant target. The head is then rotated in the direction opposite the gaze palsy. Gaze palsies caused by lesions of the cerebral cortex can typically be overcome by vestibulo-ocular testing. In prenuclear, nuclear, or infranuclear lesions, the reflex does not overcome the palsy. Vestibulo-ocular reflex testing The patient's head is tilted back 60 degrees and the external auditory meatus irrigated with either cool or warm water to stimulate the horizontal semicircular canal. When warm water is used, the fast phase is toward the stimulated ear. The mnemonic COWS (cool, opposite, warm, same) refers to the direction of the fast phase of the nystagmus. In comatose patients, no corrective (fast) phase occurs. A 40-year-old otherwise healthy African American female comes in complaining of 1 year of intermittent jumping vision and binocular diplopia with images oblique to one another. Between episodes her vision is fine. Each episodes last anywhere from a “split second” to “minutes” and episodes have become more frequently recently. The patient astutely notices that the episodes are sometimes triggered when she looks down or tilts her head to the left. Above is a video showing pertinent exam findings. What is the diagnosis in this case? ( video missing ) A.Cyclotorsional nystagmus B.Volitional nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Superior oblique myokymia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This is a classic case of superior oblique myokymia (SOM) characterized by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. SOM is almost always unilateral and in this patient is occurring in the left eye only. While some patients can recognize which eye is jumping often people are unable to describe the history in that detail. The differential diagnosis for jumping vision in one eye is very limited and almost always is caused by SOM although ocular neuromyotonia (often related to prior iatrogenic radiation exposure) would be another possibility. While the etiology of SOM is usually unknown, some cases of SOM demonstrate MRI findings of vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Other proposed theories for SOM include axonal regeneration following mild damage to the trochlear nerve (from any cause) leading to aberrant spontaneous discharges of the nerve. SOM usually causes a fine amplitude oscillatory contraction of the superior oblique muscle (as is seen in this video in the left eye). Observing the conjunctival vessels with the slit lamp will often allow the observer to clearly see small amplitude episodic incyclotorsional and infraduction movements of the affected eye. Patients experience this as monocular oscillopsia and binocular diplopia. Stressing the superior oblique muscle by head tilt towards the ipsilateral side or looking down can often trigger an event of SOM. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work- ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is typically horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. Pure cyclotorsional, or rotary, nystagmus is not a diagnosis but rather a finding that can occur due to many different etiologies. This would be expected to be bilateral and would not be worse looking down and with an ipsilateral head tilt. Square wave jerks are a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase typical of nystagmus and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or intersaccadic interval) and then a quick return to fixation. An occasional square wave jerk is physiologic but frequent square wave jerks (more than 9 per minute) raise concern for cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and progressive supranuclear palsy.

question: A 21-year-old young man presents to your clinic with acute, painless loss of vision in the right eye. His best corrected visual acuity is 20/100 and 20/20 in the right and left eyes respectively. There is an afferent pupillary defect (APD) OD. His exam is notable for hyperemia and elevation of the right optic disc but without leakage on fluorescein angiogram (FA). What is the most common visual field defect associated with this patient's likely disorder?
explanation: This young man presents with an optic neuropathy of the right eye with acutely decreased vision, an APD, and optic disc swelling. However, unlike inflammatory optic neuropathies (e.g. optic neuritis), there is no leakage on FA. His history and clinical findings are consistent with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). Other features of LHON include peripapillary telangiectasia, thickening of the peripapillary retina, and tortuosity of the medium-sized retinal arterioles. The most common visual field defect is a cecocentral defect. As discussed elsewhere in this section, LHON is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, usually at position 11778. Therefore, only mothers are capable of transmitting this disease to their offspring. The fellow eye typically has subclinical visual field abnormalities at presentation that eventually progress to mirror the first eye over the ensuing weeks or months. There is no proven treatment of this optic neuropathy. However, avoidance of tobacco and excess alcohol is probably prudent to decrease oxidative demand. An otherwise-healthy 25-year old male is assaulted by "two dudes" while "minding his own business." He was struck on the left side of the face and suffered immediate vision loss in the left eye. On testing, his vision in the right eye is 20/20 and left eye is 20/150. He has brisk pupillary reflexes without an afferent pupillary defect (APD). There is mild swelling in the left frontal region but no periocular swelling. Ocular motility is full and visual fields are full to confrontation with finger counting in both eyes. The slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable in both eyes. The patient says he knows the "two dudes" and he is going to sue them. Why does this patient definitely not have traumatic optic neuropathy (TON)? A.His vision should be worse than 20/150 with TON B.His fundus exam did not show disc edema C.He did not demonstrate an APD D.His visual field was full to confrontation High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Traumatic optic neuropathy always presents with an APD in the affected eye (assuming the contralateral eye has normal optic nerve function). TON can have mild to severe impairment of visual acuity and visual fields. Usually the damage occurs in the retrobulbar portion of the optic nerve in the optic canal so there is no disc swelling visible on fundus exam. Which of the following is NOT associated with small optic disc drusen (ODD)? A.tuberous sclerosis (TS) B.retinitis pigmentosa (RP) C.pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) D.Caucasian race High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: There seems to be a higher rate of small ODD in patients with RP and PXE. The literature suggests that in RP patients the ODD are often extruded along the margin of the optic disc providing a "scalloped" appearance and making the ODD more visible on exam. ODD rarely affects non-Caucasians. TS is associated with "mulberry-like" retinal astrocytic hamartomas. When present on the optic nerve head, astrocytic hamartomas can be confused with ODD. For the OQ over achievers who wish to learn something not currently published in the BCSC, Alagille syndrome, or arteriohepatic dysplasia, which is a disorder of familial intrahepatic cholestasis, is also highly associated with optic nerve head drusen. These patients are known to exhibit posterior embryotoxon but also usually have optic nerve head drusen. According to the initial study of 20 patients with AS that described this association, 95% had ultrasound evidence of drusen in at least one eye and 80% had bilateral optic nerve head drusen. In reality, however, most pathology that result in color vision loss (optic neuropathies / maculopathies) have a significant red-green component. These more detailed tests all involve arranging colored discs or chips in order of hue and intensity. Due to the time involved to administer them, they are seldom if ever used as screening tests. In comatose patients, no corrective (fast) phase occurs. When warm water is used, the fast phase is toward the stimulated ear. The mnemonic COWS (cool, opposite, warm, same) refers to the direction of the fast phase of the nystagmus. In comatose patients, no corrective (fast) phase occurs. A 40-year-old otherwise healthy African American female comes in complaining of 1 year of intermittent jumping vision and binocular diplopia with images oblique to one another. Between episodes her vision is fine. Each episodes last anywhere from a “split second” to “minutes” and episodes have become more frequently recently. The patient astutely notices that the episodes are sometimes triggered when she looks down or tilts her head to the left. Above is a video showing pertinent exam findings. What is the diagnosis in this case? ( video missing ) A.Cyclotorsional nystagmus B.Volitional nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Superior oblique myokymia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This is a classic case of superior oblique myokymia (SOM) characterized by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. SOM is almost always unilateral and in this patient is occurring in the left eye only. While some patients can recognize which eye is jumping often people are unable to describe the history in that detail. The differential diagnosis for jumping vision in one eye is very limited and almost always is caused by SOM although ocular neuromyotonia (often related to prior iatrogenic radiation exposure) would be another possibility. While the etiology of SOM is usually unknown, some cases of SOM demonstrate MRI findings of vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Other proposed theories for SOM include axonal regeneration following mild damage to the trochlear nerve (from any cause) leading to aberrant spontaneous discharges of the nerve. SOM usually causes a fine amplitude oscillatory contraction of the superior oblique muscle (as is seen in this video in the left eye). Observing the conjunctival vessels with the slit lamp will often allow the observer to clearly see small amplitude episodic incyclotorsional and infraduction movements of the affected eye. Patients experience this as monocular oscillopsia and binocular diplopia. Stressing the superior oblique muscle by head tilt towards the ipsilateral side or looking down can often trigger an event of SOM. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work- ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is typically horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. Pure cyclotorsional, or rotary, nystagmus is not a diagnosis but rather a finding that can occur due to many different etiologies. This would be expected to be bilateral and would not be worse looking down and with an ipsilateral head tilt. Square wave jerks are a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase typical of nystagmus and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or intersaccadic interval) and then a quick return to fixation. An occasional square wave jerk is physiologic but frequent square wave jerks (more than 9 per minute) raise concern for cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and progressive supranuclear palsy.

question: Assuming that any additional images from the MRI not shown fail to provide additional insight in this case, what is the most likely mechanism of vision loss in this patient?

options.A: Medication-related toxicity of retinal ganglion cell mitochondria
options.B: Pituitary macroadenoma-related compression of the optic chiasm
options.C: Tuberculum sellae meningioma-related compression of the optic chiasm
options.D: Demyelinating lesion of the optic chiasm

explanation: This patient is losing vision from ethambutol toxicity to the optic nerves. Ethambutol is an antimycobacterial medication used to treat tuberculosis (TB) and TB-related pathogens including myacobacterium avium complex and mycobacterium kansasii. Eye care providers must be keenly aware of ethambutol because it causes an optic neuropathy in an estimated 1.5% of patients who use it. Failure to recognize and stop the medication in Ethambutol toxicity cases will result in severe, permanent vision loss. The mechanism of vision loss in Ethambutol toxicity is related to mitochondrial toxicity of the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Typical of mitochondrial optic neuropathies, visual fields often show a cecocentral predominate pattern of vision loss with early decreased color vision and visual acuity. Interestingly, there is often a marked disparity between visual function and optic nerve appearance in these patients in that the optic nerves appear normal until late in the course of vision loss (months after onset). By the time optic pallor is seen, visual loss is more likely to be permanent. Also interesting, many patients (not rare) with Ethambutol toxicity have a bitemporal pattern of visual field loss on formal visual fields in addition to a cecocentral pattern. It is theorized that for some reason the RGCs whose axons decussate in the chiasm are more susceptible to mitochondrial toxicity similar to the RGCs of the papillomacular bundle.1 Ethambutol toxicity is one of only a handful of causes for bitemporal hemianopia with a normal MRI (assuming a correct interpretation and good quality images in the scan). The vast majority of bitemporal hemianopia cases will be explained by structural abnormality seen on a good quality MRI. This patient’s coronal MRI image through the optic chiasm and pituitary is normal. There is no mass seen compressing or elevating the chiasm as we would expect if there were a meningioma or pituitary macroadenoma as the cause of her vision loss. When there is a mass compressing the optic chiasm, the MRI findings are typically not subtle. Demyelination of the optic chiasm as compared to the optic nerve is quite unusual. When it does occur, it is more common in association with neuro-myelitis optica than with multiple sclerosis. A new demyelinating lesion in a 70-year-old patient without a history of a demyelinating disease would be exceedingly rare and we would expect to see some enhancement of the optic chiasm on post- contrast T1 images (which we do not see in this case). In case you need to refresh your midline brain anatomy, please see our diagram below. A is the internal carotid artery in the cavernous sinus, B is the optic chiasm, C is a normal pituitary gland, and D is the sphenoid sinus. 1 http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21597402 A 23-year-old otherwise healthy Caucasian female presents with acute painful vision loss in the right eye that started 2 days ago. Her pain is worse with eye movement. Uncorrected she has 20/100 vision in the right eye and 20/20 vision in the left with a brisk right afferent pupillary defect. Her slit lamp and dilated fundus exam are unremarkable. Above are two slices from her MRI. On the left is a coronal T2 FLAIR sequence image through the retrobulbar orbits and on the right is a coronal T1 post-contrast image through the retrobulbar orbits. According to the optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT), what is this patient’s 10-year risk of multiple sclerosis (assuming the remaining MRI images NOT SHOWN ABOVE fail to reveal any additional pathology)? A.11% B.22% C.38% D.56% Topic: Optic Nerve High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This question stem describes the classic presentation of demyelinating optic neuritis in a young Caucasian female who fits the demographic for multiple sclerosis (MS). Note that the vision loss is painful, there is a marked right afferent pupillary defect, and that the right optic nerve is normal appearing (which is true about two thirds of optic neuritis cases). The optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT) showed that the long-term risk for development of MS can be assessed in patients with isolated optic neuritis based on the presence or absence of characteristic demyelinating white matter changes on MRI of the brain. A patient with isolated optic neuritis and no characteristic white matter changes on MRI of the brain has a 22% risk of MS development in 10 years. This risk climbs to 56% in 10 years for patients with one or more white matter lesions. The 10-year risk for MS development among all patients with a single bout of clinically isolated optic neuritis (not taking into account MRI findings) is 38%. This information can be remembered as the "10/20/40/60 rule." MRI of the orbits (in addition to the brain) is often performed in patients to confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimickers but according to neuro-op mantra, is not necessary for the clinical diagnosis of optic neuritis in typical cases such as this. The MRI images provided in this case are likewise classic for demyelinating optic neuritis. In image on the right, we can see post contrast enhancement of the right retrobulbar optic nerve as compared to the left which is characteristic of but not specific for demyelinating optic neuritis. (Yes, the enhancement is subtle, but it is present). If there is any doubt about the enhancement, the left MRI image which shows a FLAIR sequence taken further posterior than the right coronal image shows T2 hyperintensity of the right optic nerve which is also a characteristic and non-specific finding of demyelinating optic neuritis. The key to answering this challenging question correctly is recognizing the T2 FLAIR hyperintensity in the left frontal lobe adjacent to the lateral ventricle. This lesion is quite large in size and its periventricular location make it characteristic of a demyelinating lesion. Because we don’t have a T1 post-contrast MRI image through the same area to see if it is enhancing, there is insufficient information given to say whether the left frontal lobe lesion is new or old. Regardless, the presence of a typical white matter lesion on the coronal FLAIR lesion gives this patient a 56% 10-year and a 72% 15-year risk for MS according to the ONTT. In case you are lost looking at MRIs, the images are shown again below with white arrows indicating key pathology.

question: Which of the following is the most important distinguishing feature between acute papilledema (optic disc edema due to elevated intracranial pressure) and acute optic disc edema from other causes?

options.A: The presence or absence of optic nerve hyperemia
options.B: The presence or absence of optic nerve gliosis
options.C: The visual function of the optic nerve in question (acuity, fields, color vision)
options.D: The presence or absence of peripapillary hemorrhages Topic: Optic Nerve

explanation: Papilledema (optic disc edema due to increased intracranial pressure) and optic disc edema due to other causes (ischemia, demyelination, optic nerve infiltration, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, etc) are indistinguishable based on appearance. In the acute phase, both demonstrate hyperemia and blurring of the disc margins due to swelling in the nerve fiber layer. Both can demonstrate peripapillary hemorrhages. Optic nerve "gliosis" is a characteristic finding in chronically swollen optic nerves with a glistening grayish appearance that can make the disc look elevated forever. When assessing a swollen optic nerve it is important to note the correlation between disc swelling and visual function. Generally, papilledema is bilateral and patients retain good visual function (central visual acuity, visual fields, and color vision) until late in the disease course regardless of how swollen the nerve appears. Optic disc edema from other causes often has prominent visual field and/or acuity deficits early in the disease course. In these instances, the visual field and acuity can be much worse than expected based on the optic nerve appearance.

question: A 70-year-old Caucasian male presents to your clinic because his wife recently noticed that his pupils were different sized. You examine the patient and note anisocoria that is greater in the dark compared to the light. The top photo shows the patient’s exam before you apply drops in both eyes to confirm your suspected diagnosis. The bottom photo shows the patient’s exam 30 minutes after drop application. Which pupil is abnormal and what drops were applied?
explanation: Anisocoria that is greater in the dark than the light suggests that there is abnormal dilation under dark conditions. That means that the smaller pupil would be the suspect pupil. While subtle, this patient’s exam clearly shows 1-2 mm of right upper eyelid ptosis in the right eye with the miotic pupil. Together these features are concerning for Horner syndrome in the right eye. Drop testing was performed to confirm the diagnosis. Technically there are three drops that can aide in the work-up of Horner syndrome; cocaine and apraclonidine can be used to confirm the diagnosis and hydroxyamphetamine can be used to localize the pathology to either the first/second-order neuron or the third-order neuron. In reality, hydroxyamphetamine drops are no longer available in the US market except from special order pharmacies so this test has been abandoned by most clinicians. Historically the most commonly utilized drop test for the confirmation of Horner syndrome was cocaine testing although regulations on cocaine have led to more clinicians using apraclonidine drop testing. The response of a normal pupil to cocaine 10% is dilation because cocaine blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the pre-synaptic cleft allowing more norepinephrine to function in stimulation of the pupillary dilator muscle. The response of a Horner syndrome pupil to cocaine is no or poor dilation because of decreased sympathetic tone to the eye there is a shortage of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft. Despite blockage of pre-synaptic norepinephrine reuptake by cocaine in a Horner syndrome eye, there is limited norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft to cause dilation. If anisocoria is physiologic both pupils will dilate equally (or nearly equally) leading to less than 1 mm anisocoria 30 minutes following instillation of cocaine 10% in both eyes. In this patient with a right Horner syndrome, a cocaine test would have resulted in an increase in the anisocoria with the left eye dilating and the right eye staying about the same size. Apraclonidine is an alpha-adrenergic receptor agonist that has more effect on alpha-2 receptors than alpha-1 receptors. It is not completely clear how it functions in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome but the current theory revolves around up-regulation of post-synaptic alpha-1 receptors in Horner syndrome. The belief is that as early as 36 hours following disruption of sympathetic fibers to the eye, the pupillary dilator muscle experiences up-regulation of alpha-1 receptors in response to sympathetic denervation. A normal pupillary response to apraclonidine (trade name Iopidine) is mild constriction due to action of the medication on pre-synaptic alpha-2 receptors which act to decrease release of norepinephrine to the dilator muscle. In patients with Horner syndrome, however, the action of apraclonidine on up- regulated alpha-1 receptors predominates over the presynaptic alpha-2 effect resulting in dilation. In an individual with unilateral Horner syndrome who has apraclonidine drops applied bilaterally, the abnormal eye dilates and the normal eye constricts leading to reversal of anisocoria as seen in this patient. Which of the following would NOT be expected to result in light-near dissociation? A.Cerebellar degeneration with downbeat nystagmus B.Severe proliferative diabetic retinopathy status post extensive PRP laser OU C.Bilateral arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy with HM vision OU D.Neuro-syphilis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Light-near dissociation (LND) occurs when the most pronounced pupillary constriction to light is less than the most pronounced pupillary constriction upon near gaze. There are numerous locations along the pupillary light reflex pathway where pathology can result in light-near dissociation. The most common cause of LND is bilateral loss of afferent input from the retina / optic nerves to the pupillary light reflex. Because the near response reflex (convergence, miosis, and accommodation) does not rely on afferent input from photoreceptors to cause pupillary constriction, patients with vision loss from severe retina or optic nerve disease will exhibit limited pupillary response to light but retain pupillary constriction with near response. Neuro-syphilis can cause Argyll-Robertson pupils or Adie's tonic pupils; both of which demonstrate light near dissociation. In Argyll-Robertson pupils, there are small irregular pupils (usually bilateral) which are poorly responsive to light but constrict to near response. Exceedingly rare in modern medical practice, the pathophysiology of Argyll-Robertson pupils remains unclear although some theorize that there is disruption of pupillary light input to the Edinger-Westphal in the dorsal midbrain. Adie's tonic pupil causes LND due to aberrant regeneration of ciliary body parasympathetic input responsible for accommodation. Following disruption of post-synaptic parasympathetics from the ciliary ganglion, accommodative parasympathetics regenerate and aberrantly innervate the pupillary constrictor muscle causing a relative increase in constriction with near response as opposed to light response. Finally, Parinaud's (or dorsal midbrain) syndrome is another cause of LND by disruption of pupillary light input to the Edinger-Westphal in the dorsal midbrain. This mechanism is similar to the proposed pathophysiology underlying Argyll-Robertson pupils but in the case of Parinaud's syndrome, the etiology is usually compressive from a mass and/or hydrocephalus. What exam finding suggests a congenital or longstanding Horner syndrome in a patient with right upper eyelid ptosis and relative miosis of the right pupil? A.Anhidrosis of the right side of the face B.Poor levator function of the right ptotic eyelid C.Impaired visual acuity of the right eye D.Hypopigmentation of the right iris Correct Answer: D Explanation: Sympathetic innervation is required for normal melanocyte development within the iris. In cases of congenital Horner's or in isolated cases of long standing Horner syndrome from childhood, the iris on the affected side is often hypopigmented in comparison to the normal contralateral iris (one cause of "iris heterochromia"). Anhidrosis, or absence of sweating, occurs in association with Horner syndrome to varying degrees depending on the level of the interruption in the sympathetic pathway. In 1st order lesions, anhidrosis affects the entire ipsilateral half of the body. In 2nd order lesions, anhidrosis typically affects the involved half of the face. In 3rd order lesions, anhidrosis may or may not occur; when present it is usually isolated to the ipsilateral brow. Horner syndrome should not affect visual acuity. Disruption of sympathetic input to Muller's muscle results in mild ipsilateral upper eyelid ptosis (about 1-2 mm) and would have minimal impact on levator function measurements. Neither levator function nor anhidrosis helps to distinguish long standing Horner syndrome from more acute disease.

question: Which of the following is the most likely etiology for his heterochromia?
explanation: All of the answer choices are causes of heterochromia. Neuroblastoma and birth trauma- related brachial plexus injuries both cause Horner syndrome. This child shows heterochromia with a lighter colored left iris, anisocoria with a smaller left pupil, and a smaller palpebral fissure on the left indicative of a left Horner syndrome. Of note, sometimes on examination the narrowing of the palpebral fissure from a combination of subtle upper eyelid ptosis and lower eyelid inverse ptosis is more prominent than upper eyelid ptosis. Sympathetic innervation is required for normal melanocyte development within the iris. In cases of congenital Horner syndrome or in acquired Horner syndrome from early childhood, the iris on the affected side is often hypopigmented in comparison to the normal contralateral iris. Birth trauma to the brachial plexus from challenging vaginal deliveries (i.e. shoulder dystocia) is a very common cause of congenital Horner syndrome. Another associated feature of brachial plexus injury is arm weakness. Neuroblastoma can present with seemingly isolated Horner syndrome and can also present with a Horner syndrome demonstrating iris heterochromia suggesting that it was present from very early in life. Without a history of birth trauma and associated arm weakness this patient would require a work-up to rule-out neuroblastoma. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis can cause heterochromia from chronic inflammation of the anterior segment with iris stromal atrophy. Usually the heterochromia would present later in life after the inflammation had sufficient time to cause iris atrophy. Additionally Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis would not be expected to cause ptosis, anisocoria, or arm weakness. Waardenberg syndrome is a rare genetic disorder caused by abnormal neural crest migration and is marked by sensorineural deafness, dystopia canthorum, heterochromia, and a white forelock of hair arising from the anterior scalp. How does cocaine function to aid in diagnosis of Horner syndrome? A.It blocks re-uptake of norepinephrine at the pre-synaptic terminal B.It blocks re-uptake of acetylcholine at the pre-synaptic terminal C.It causes release of stored norepinephrine at the pre-synaptic terminal D.It causes release of stored acetylcholine at the pre-synaptic terminal High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Throughout the entire nervous system, cocaine functions by blocking re-uptake of catecholamines such as dopamine and norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the pre- synaptic nerve terminal. In the eye this results in more norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft causing contraction of the pupil dilator muscle and subsequent dilation. Acetylcholine is the neuro-transmitter utilized by the parasympathetic autonomic system and in the eye would trigger contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle to cause miosis. In Horner syndrome there is a lack of normal sympathetic tone to the eye. The effect of cocaine on a normal eye is dilation but in an eye with Horner syndrome there is a diminished or absent effect. When instilled bilaterally in a patient with a unilateral Horner syndrome, the involved eye will have little response while the normal eye will dilate thus increasing anisocoria. Greater than 0.8-1 mm of anisocoria 30 minutes following application of cocaine drops (usually 10%) is diagnostic of Horner syndrome in the more miotic eye (assuming there is no intrinsic iris abnormality preventing normal dilation such as posterior synechiae). A 30-year-old female presents with a dilated left pupil that she first noticed while applying make-up one week ago. She denies any associated eye pain, headache, diplopia, or ptosis but she feels like her near vision is blurry in the left eye. She denies any recent eye drops, takes no medications, and has suffered no ocular trauma in the past. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU at distance with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is slightly irregular (oval), measures about 8 mm in the dark, and is sluggishly reactive to light to 7 mm. With near gaze the patient has sluggish constriction of the left pupil to about 4 mm. After relaxation of near gaze there is a delayed re-dilation of the left pupil relative to the normal right pupil. The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing). Which of the following would confirm the most likely diagnosis in this patient? explanation: Throughout the entire nervous system, cocaine functions by blocking re-uptake of catecholamines such as dopamine and norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the pre- synaptic nerve terminal. question: Which of the following is an etiology of the patient’s condition?
explanation: The major causes of anisocoria organized by a defect in dilation (defect in the sympathetic pathway) versus constriction (defect in the parasympathetic pathway) are shown in the image along with pharmacologic testing and clues to the diagnosis. The patient is presenting with a tonic pupil. Tonic pupils typically present with the patient noting pupil asymmetry when looking in the mirror. The patient may be symptomatic due to photophobia or difficulty reading. Initially, the pupil is dilated, and exhibits light-near dissociation with redilation lag. Additionally, corneal sensation may be depressed. The pupil on slit-lamp examination may be irregular with sectoral paralysis. C hronically, the pupil can become constricted compared to the fellow pupil. The pathophysiology of a tonic pupil is damage to the ciliary ganglion or the postganglionic short ciliary nerves that innervate the iris sphincter and ciliary muscles. Partial preservation of innervation leads to the sectoral paralysis that is characteristic of a tonic pupil. The light-near dissociation is explained by the 30:1 ratio of accommodative fibers to light responsive fibers leading to a greater chance of loss of constriction to light with relative preservation of accommodation. Iris sphincter denervation leads to a hypersensitivity response to cholinergic agents. Therefore, the diagnosis can be aided with dilute (0.125%) pilocarpine. Normal pupils will not constrict much to dilute pilocarpine, and the test is considered positive if the abnormal pupil constricts more than the fellow pupil. The causes of a tonic pupil include: 1. Adie tonic pupil: a syndrome consisting of a tonic pupil and absent deep tendon reflexes. 2. Local damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves: trauma, viral infiltration, orbital tumors, sarcoidosis, and ischemic processes such as giant cell arteritis. 3. As a presentation of autonomic dysfunction: neurosyphilis, advanced diabetes, dysautonomia syndromes, Guillain-Barré syndrome / Miller fisher syndrome among many others. 4. Idiopathic In the absence of other associated signs or symptoms, syphilis testing or ESR/CRP in elderly patients should be considered in the workup of tonic pupils as neurosyphilis and giant cell arteritis may be the underlying cause. Otherwise, no other workup is typically required as most cases are benign. Patients are rarely treated with dilute pilocarpine or pupil-forming contact lenses to aid accommodation and treat photophobia. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice B): A carotid artery dissection is a potential etiology of Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome (oculosympathetic paresis) can consist of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis due to a lesion in the three-neuron sympathetic pathway that originates in the hypothalamus, travels down and up the neck, and terminates at the pupillary dilator. Ocular signs include mild upper lid ptosis (denervation of muller’s muscle), reverse ptosis of the lower lid (denervation of lower lid retractors), and dilation lag. Pharmacologic testing using apraclonidine (alpha- adrenergic receptor agonist) can confirm the diagnosis with reversal of anisocoria as the denervated pupillary dilator is hypersensitive and will dilate widely to alpha- adrenergic agonists. Additionally, 10% cocaine (norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) will not cause dilation of a Horner pupil as the denervated sympathetic third-order neuron is not releasing neurotransmitter, whereas it will cause dilation of a normal pupil. • (Choice C): A pharmacologic dilation pupil will not respond to dilute pilocarpine or 1% pilocarpine. • (Choice D): A posterior communicating artery aneurysm is a cause of a third-nerve palsy. In addition to loss of pupillary sphincter function, a third-nerve palsy presents with ptosis and motility defects due to paresis of the superior, inferior, and medial recti; inferior oblique; and levator palpebrae superioris. Dilute pilocarpine rarely causes constriction of an acute third-nerve palsy pupil and can be used to distinguish a third-nerve palsy from a tonic pupil. However, a chronically dilated pupil from a third-nerve palsy can sometimes be difficult to distinguish as both may demonstrate denervation hypersensitivity, light-near dissociation, and segmental paralysis Benign episodic pupillary mydriasis is associated with what neurological condition? A.Adie's tonic pupil B.Myasthenia gravis C.Trigeminal neuralgia D.Migraine headaches High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: While other more serious causes of mydriasis should always be considered before arriving at a diagnosis of benign episodic pupillary mydriasis, it is a well-described explanation for intermittent mydriasis. The majority of patients with benign episodic pupillary mydriasis have a history of migraine headaches. Similar to the "tad pole" pupil associated with migraine headaches, bouts of pupillary mydriasis do not necessarily have to be temporally associated with migraine headaches. Pupil mydriasis usually lasts minutes to hours and may occur before, after, or randomly in relation to headaches. As the name suggests, the condition is "benign" without other associated neurological deficits. There are many intraocular causes for irregular pupils including prior intraocular surgery with focal iris damage, peripheral anterior or posterior synecheie, iris colobomas, iris sphincter tears, iridodialysis, and neovascularization of the iris. What two neurological disorders are associated with an irregularly shaped pupil? A.Midbrain pathology and migraine B.Midbrain pathology and myasthenia gravis C.Migraine and optic nerve meningioma D.Myasthenia gravis and internuclear ophthalmoplegia High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: "Midbrain corectopia" and migraine associated "tadpole pupil" are two causes of irregular pupils associated with neurologic disease. Midbrain corectopia is rare but usually results from diffuse damage to the midbrain which is thought to cause selective inhibition of portions of pupillomotor fibers from the Edinger- Westphal nucleus. Most cases in the literature have been bilateral and the degree of correctopia may fluctuate. One case showed 5-15 minute cycles of correctopia followed by resolution. Migraine associated "tadpole pupils" is a benign disorder that typically occurs in one eye and includes a sectoral dilation or spasm of the pupil lasting a few minutes. The pupillary events may or may not be associated with a migraine headache but patients with "tadpole pupils" often have a history of migraine headache disorder. Which of the following disease entities would be expected to result in a 2nd-order Horner syndrome? A.Wallenberg syndrome secondary to ischemic stroke B.Cluster headache C.A lung cancer metastasis to the cavernous sinus D.A thoracic aortic aneurysm High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: D Explanation: The sympathetic pathway to the eye is complex and involves three interconnected neuron segments (first order, second order, and third order). Throughout the entire sympathetic pathway, axons never decussate meaning that causative lesions are always ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome. The cell bodies of the first order neuron lies in the posterior lateral hypothalamus and descends through the brainstem to the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 where they synapse with cell bodies of the second order neurons. Wallenberg (or lateral medullary syndrome) usually arises from a stroke and causes a first order Horner syndrome. Other causes of first order Horner syndrome include thalamic hemorrhage / stroke and tumors, cervical disc disease, demyelination, and other pathology of the cervical spinal cord. Second order sympathetic neurons project from the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 to the paravertebral sympathetic chain where fibers ascend to the superior cervical ganglion and synapse with third order neurons. Causes of a second order Horner syndrome include apical lung malignancies ("Pancoast syndrome"), thoracic aortic aneurysms, brachial plexus injuries, and thoracic surgery with disruption of the superior portion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain. Third order neuron cell bodies lie in the superior cervical ganglion and pass superiorly into the cranial cavity with the internal carotid artery (ICA) in a fine web of nerves along the wall of the artery known as the carotid plexus. The ocular sympathetics continue with the internal carotid as it passes through the cavernous sinus. While in the cavernous sinus, the third order neuron axons travel from the ICA to the abducens nerve before joining the nasociliary branch of V1. The sympathetics then travel with the nasociliary branch of V1 into the orbit and through the ciliary ganglion (without synapsing) to extend to the dilator muscle of the eye. Causes of third order Horner syndrome include internal carotid artery pathology (including dissection), cavernous sinus compressive / inflammatory lesions, and trigeminal autonomic cephalgia type headaches (e.g. cluster headache, SUNCT, etc). A patient with lung cancer of the right upper lobe has right upper eyelid ptosis and anisocoria that is greater in the dark with a right miotic pupil. What is the best definition of a positive cocaine test for unilateral Horner syndrome? A.No dilation OD 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OD only B.< 1 mm dilation OD 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OD only C.Reversal of anisocoria 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OU D.> 1 mm anisocoria 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OU High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Drop testing to confirm the diagnosis of Horner syndrome is important in clinical practice and on standardized tests. Historically, the most commonly utilized drop test for the confirmation of Horner syndrome is cocaine testing. The response of a normal pupil to cocaine 10% is dilation because cocaine blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the pre-synaptic cleft allowing more norepinephrine to function in stimulation of the pupillary dilator muscle. The response of a Horner syndrome pupil to cocaine is no or poor dilation because there is a shortage of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft. Despite blockage of pre-synaptic norepinephrine reuptake by cocaine in a Horner syndrome eye, there is already limited norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft to cause dilation. The most accurate means to measure a positive response, therefore, is a relative comparison of dilation between the two eyes. If anisocoria is physiologic, for instance, both pupils will dilate equally (or nearly equally) leading to less than 1 mm anisocoria 30 minutes following instillation of cocaine 10% in both eyes. Of note, "reversal of anisocoria" indicates Horner syndrome following application of apraclonidine 1%. In other words, the Horner syndrome pupil will dilate much more than the normal pupil after instillation of apraclonidine. This phenomenon occurs since the Horner iris dilator muscle develops adrenergic supersensitivity. This fact is quite useful since apraclonidine is typically easier to obtain than cocaine in most eye clinics. What percentage of the general population has physiologic anisocoria noticeable on penlight examination? A.1% B.5% C.10% D.20% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: This is a fact that should be memorized. Anisocoria can be appreciated reliably on clinical examination when a 0.2 mm to 0.4 mm difference in pupillary diameter occurs. There is almost always less than 1 mm difference in pupillary diameter in physiologic anisocoria although greater disparities can occur. The classic teaching is that physiologic anisocoria (PA) is the same in light and dark conditions although there are exceptions. Some cases of PA can show more pronounced anisocoria in dark lighting. In that case, cocaine testing would help distinguish PA from Horner's syndrome because both eyes will dilate equally in response to cocaine while in Horner's syndrome the abnormal smaller pupil does not respond equally to cocaine . Cluster headaches and carotid dissections can both be causes of ipsilateral Horner's syndromes and would be expected to result in an anisocoria that is greater in dark due to impaired sympathetic input on the side of the lesion causing a miotic pupil with abnormal dilation. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can cause an ipsilateral pupil involving third nerve palsy due to compressive impairment of pupillomotor fibers running in the peripheral / external portion of the third nerve. This would be expected to cause anisocoria that is greater in light conditions due to impaired parasympathetic pupillary constriction in the larger pupil.

explanation: "Midbrain corectopia" and migraine associated "tadpole pupil" are two causes of irregular pupils associated with neurologic disease. Midbrain corectopia is rare but usually results from diffuse damage to the midbrain which is thought to cause selective inhibition of portions of pupillomotor fibers from the Edinger- Westphal nucleus. explanation: This scenario is meant to simulate the anxious frenzy that frequently surrounds the care of patients with a unilateral dilated pupil. In these situations medical care providers not accustomed to evaluating anisocoria are trained to first think of CN3 palsy from brainstem herniation or posterior communicating artery aneurysm. The truth is that CN 3 palsy virtually never presents as an isolated dilated pupil. It is important to assess carefully for signs of a partial pupil involving CN 3 palsy by checking motility, alignment with alternate cover testing or Maddox rod, and ptosis. If the deficit is truly an isolated dilated pupil, however, everyone should relax. Patients with uncal herniation causing CN 3 palsy always have altered mental status excluding that possibility in this case. MRA and CTA are both excellent tests to rule-out aneurysm as the cause of a pupil involving CN 3 palsy but they are not indicated in this case. With the information provided in the question, the most likely causes include a right tonic pupil (referred to by some as an Adies pupil) or medication induced mydriasis. Dilute pilocarpine testing with 0.1% or 0.125% pilocarpine will allow assessment of supersensitivity of the right pupil. Constriction to dilute pilocarpine is indicative (but not diagnostic) of a tonic pupil. The dilute pilocarpine is usually applied in both eyes so the contralateral eye serves as a control. If there is no appreciable response to dilute pilocarpine then pilocarpine 1% can be placed in both eyes; if the right eye fails to constrict then the cause of mydriasis is medication. If the results of drop testing are inconclusive then the safest option is to have the patient return the next day for repeat evaluation and possible repeat drop testing. In those super rare cases of CN 3 palsy from an aneurysm presenting with isolated pupillary mydriasis, other signs/findings of CN3 palsy will generally appear within several days. following the observation of anisocoria, the above pharmacological tests are carried out. What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Preganglionic Horner’s B.Post-ganglionic Horner’s C.Holme’s Aides pupil D.Pharmacological mydriasis High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Horner syndrome pharmacological investigations Cocaine 4%: the normal pupil will dilate, but a Horner pupil will not. A positive test is typically defined as more than 1 mm of anisocoria after drops are instilled in both eyes (with the smaller pupil being the abnormal Horner eye). Hydroxyamphetamine 1%: for a pre-ganglionic lesion (1st or 2nd order Horner syndrome), the pupil will dilate whereas in a post-ganglionic lesion (3rd order) it will not dilate. Adrenaline 1:1000: for a preganglionic lesion, the pupil will fail to dilate whereas in a postganglionic lesion it will dilate. Phenylephrine 2.5% and 10% are typically used for dilation. Dilute phenylephrine (1%) has little if any dilation effect on a normal iris. In a sympathetically de-innervated pupils (Horner syndrome) there is suprasensitivity and the pupil will dilate. Much like apraclonidine 0.5% or 1% testing this may lead to a reversal of anisocoria. A 60-year-old female presents with anisocoria which she noticed one week prior to presentation while looking in the mirror. Her right pupil is significantly smaller than her left. She also noticed drooping of her right eyelid for the past year. She feels like her vision is slightly blurry in her left eye for the past 6 months although admits that her current glasses are 2 years old. She has a history of migraine headaches for about 35 years which are usually left sided and last for several hours before subsiding. There is a strong family history of migraines. The patient denies any headaches in the last week. If your exam confirms the presence of anisocoria, what single finding is the most important in elucidating the underlying etiology of her anisocoria? A.The presence of ptosis B.The effect of lighting conditions on her anisocoria C.The presence of visual blurring D.The location of her headache High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This may seem like a silly question but it is important conceptually. The most important step in distinguishing the cause of anisocoria is whether the anisocoria is greater in light or dark. Anisocoria which is greater in dark is indicative of a failure to dilate in the more miotic pupil and may signify an number of different entities including Horner's syndrome, old chronic Adies pupil, pharmacologic miosis, or posterior synechiae. Anisocoria which is greater in light is indicative of a failure to constrict in the more mydriatic pupil and may occur with a tonic pupil, CN3 palsy, or pharmacologic mydriasis. Ptosis in the setting of anisocoria is important, but it can occur in association with miosis (Horner's syndrome) or mydriasis (CN3 palsy); so it is key to figure out whether the smaller pupil or the larger pupil is the abnormal pupil. Furthermore, ptosis is extremely common in older patients due to an age-related dehiscence of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle so it could be entirely unrelated to the anisocoria. Visual blurring, likewise, should be noted but is a common complaint and may or may not be related to the underlying anisocoria. Finally, headache is another symptom that may be related to anisocoria but is an extremely common complaint among all patients. A 45-year-old female with chronic back and neck pain presents with a drooping of her right upper eyelid for the last 2 weeks. She first noted the problem after a visit to her chiropractor for manipulation. She also notes an associated moderate right sided headache although she has a history of migraines in the past. Her vision is 20/20 OU with no afferent pupillary defect. She has anisocoria that is greater in dark and the right pupil is smaller than the left. The remainder of her neurological and ophthalmic examination is normal aside from 2 mm of right upper eyelid ptosis. Apraclonidine 0.5% applied to both eyes resulted in reversal of anisocoria and resolution of her right upper eyelid ptosis. What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient? A.MRI / MRA of the head and neck B.Immediate anticoagulation C.Reassurance D.Tensilon test High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient has right upper eyelid ptosis with miosis suggestive of Horner syndrome. Drop testing with apraclonidine showed reversal of anisocoria which confirms the diagnosis. Her history of recent chiropractic manipulation and an ipsilateral headache is very concerning for carotid artery dissection which is considered a neuro-ophthalmic emergency due to the risk for CVA. MRI / MRA of the head and neck is the appropriate study to assess for carotid dissection. The treatment of carotid dissection is controversial and depends on clinician preference and the acuteness of onset. Some experts advocate anticoagulation for stroke prevention but anticoagulation is not the correct answer choice because the diagnosis of carotid dissection should be confirmed prior to initiating treatment. question: If your exam confirms the presence of anisocoria, what single finding is the most important in elucidating the underlying etiology of her anisocoria?

options.B: The effect of lighting conditions on her anisocoria

explanation: This may seem like a silly question but it is important conceptually. The most important step in distinguishing the cause of anisocoria is whether the anisocoria is greater in light or dark. Anisocoria which is greater in dark is indicative of a failure to dilate in the more miotic pupil and may signify an number of different entities including Horner's syndrome, old chronic Adies pupil, pharmacologic miosis, or posterior synechiae. Anisocoria which is greater in light is indicative of a failure to constrict in the more mydriatic pupil and may occur with a tonic pupil, CN3 palsy, or pharmacologic mydriasis. Ptosis in the setting of anisocoria is important, but it can occur in association with miosis (Horner's syndrome) or mydriasis (CN3 palsy); so it is key to figure out whether the smaller pupil or the larger pupil is the abnormal pupil. Furthermore, ptosis is extremely common in older patients due to an age-related dehiscence of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle so it could be entirely unrelated to the anisocoria. Visual blurring, likewise, should be noted but is a common complaint and may or may not be related to the underlying anisocoria. Finally, headache is another symptom that may be related to anisocoria but is an extremely common complaint among all patients. She denies any associated headache, diplopia, or ptosis. She also denies any recent eye drops and takes no medications. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is perfectly round, measures 8 mm in the dark, and is non-reactive to light (confirmed with the slit lamp). The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing. There is no constriction of the left pupil with near gaze. You suspect that the patient has placed dilating drops in her left eye. Which of the following would definitively confirm the diagnosis of pharmacologic dilation? A.No pupillary response to pilocarpine 0.125% in the left eye B.Dramatic pupillary constriction to pilocarpine 0.125% in the left eye C.No pupillary response to pilocarpine 1% in the left eye D.Dramatic pupillary constriction to pilocarpine 1% in the left eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Fortunately the differential for a poorly reactive or non-reactive dilated pupil is limited. Possible causes include tonic pupil (sometimes referred to as Adies tonic pupil), trauma, CN3 palsy, and pharmacologic dilation (intended or unintended). Tonic pupils demonstrate denervation hypersensitivity by constricting with dilute pilocarpine 0.125%. A normal pupil and pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy will both constrict to full strength pilocarpine 1% while a pharmacologically dilated pupil will not. A severely injured iris from trauma may not constrict well in response to full strength pilocarpine but usually there are obvious signs of iris trauma on examination in addition to a history of trauma. Pharmacologic dilation may be intentional in patients seeking attention or other secondary gains or it may be unintentional in patients using scopolamine patches or "get the red out" artificial tears. Farmers / gardeners may be exposed to plant materials with dilation properties (e.g. the deadly nightshade plant). Which of the following is true regarding Horner syndrome? A.Sympathetic pathway lesions are always ipsilateral to the side of the Horner syndrome B.Pancoast tumors are a common cause of third order Horner syndrome C.The most common cause of congenital Horner syndrome is neuroblastoma D.In the cavernous sinus the sympathetics travel in closest proximity to CN4 High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The sympathetic pathway to the eye is complex and involves three interconnected neuron segments (first order, second order, and third order). Throughout the entire sympathetic pathway, axons never decussate meaning that causative lesions are always ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome. The cell bodies of the first order neuron lies in the posterior lateral hypothalamus and descends through the brainstem to the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 where they synapse with cell bodies of the second order neurons. Wallenberg (or lateral medullary syndrome) usually arises from a stroke and causes a first order Horner syndrome. Other causes of first order Horner syndrome include thalamic hemorrhage / stroke and tumors, cervical disc disease, demyelination, and other pathology of the cervical spinal cord. Second order sympathetic neurons project from the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 to the paravertebral sympathetic chain where fibers ascend to the superior cervical ganglion and synapse with third order neurons. Causes of a second order Horner syndrome include apical lung malignancies ("Pancoast syndrome"), thoracic aortic aneurysms, brachial plexus injuries, and thoracic surgery with disruption of the superior portion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain. Third order neuron cell bodies lie in the superior cervical ganglion and pass superiorly into the cranial cavity with the internal carotid artery (ICA) in a fine web of nerves along the wall of the artery known as the carotid plexus. The ocular sympathetics continue with the internal carotid as it passes through the cavernous sinus. While in the cavernous sinus, the third order neuron axons travel from the ICA to the abducens nerve before joining the nasociliary branch of V1. The sympathetics then travel with the nasociliary branch of V1 into the orbit and through the ciliary ganglion (without synapsing) to extend to the dilator muscle of the eye. Causes of third order Horner syndrome include internal carotid artery pathology (including dissection), cavernous sinus compressive / inflammatory lesions, and trigeminal autonomic cephalgia type headaches (e.g. cluster headache, SUNCT, etc).
