options.B: Pancoast tumors are a common cause of third order Horner syndrome
options.C: The most common cause of congenital Horner syndrome is neuroblastoma
options.D: In the cavernous sinus the sympathetics travel in closest proximity to CN4

explanation: The sympathetic pathway to the eye is complex and involves three interconnected neuron segments (first order, second order, and third order). Throughout the entire sympathetic pathway, axons never decussate meaning that causative lesions are always ipsilateral to the Horner syndrome. The cell bodies of the first order neuron lies in the posterior lateral hypothalamus and descends through the brainstem to the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 where they synapse with cell bodies of the second order neurons. Wallenberg (or lateral medullary syndrome) usually arises from a stroke and causes a first order Horner syndrome. Other causes of first order Horner syndrome include thalamic hemorrhage / stroke and tumors, cervical disc disease, demyelination, and other pathology of the cervical spinal cord. Second order sympathetic neurons project from the intermediolateral cell column between C7 and T2 to the paravertebral sympathetic chain where fibers ascend to the superior cervical ganglion and synapse with third order neurons. Causes of a second order Horner syndrome include apical lung malignancies ("Pancoast syndrome"), thoracic aortic aneurysms, brachial plexus injuries, and thoracic surgery with disruption of the superior portion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain. Third order neuron cell bodies lie in the superior cervical ganglion and pass superiorly into the cranial cavity with the internal carotid artery (ICA) in a fine web of nerves along the wall of the artery known as the carotid plexus. The ocular sympathetics continue with the internal carotid as it passes through the cavernous sinus. While in the cavernous sinus, the third order neuron axons travel from the ICA to the abducens nerve before joining the nasociliary branch of V1. The sympathetics then travel with the nasociliary branch of V1 into the orbit and through the ciliary ganglion (without synapsing) to extend to the dilator muscle of the eye. Causes of third order Horner syndrome include internal carotid artery pathology (including dissection), cavernous sinus compressive / inflammatory lesions, and trigeminal autonomic cephalgia type headaches (e.g. cluster headache, SUNCT, etc). A 45-year-old female with chronic back and neck pain presents with a drooping of her right upper eyelid for the last 2 weeks. She first noted the problem after a visit to her chiropractor for manipulation. She also notes an associated moderate right sided headache although she has a history of migraines in the past. Her vision is 20/20 OU with no afferent pupillary defect. She has anisocoria that is greater in dark and the right pupil is smaller than the left. The remainder of her neurological and ophthalmic examination is normal aside from 2 mm of right upper eyelid ptosis. Apraclonidine 0.5% applied to both eyes resulted in reversal of anisocoria and resolution of her right upper eyelid ptosis. What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient? A.MRI / MRA of the head and neck B.Immediate anticoagulation C.Reassurance D.Tensilon test High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient has right upper eyelid ptosis with miosis suggestive of Horner syndrome. Drop testing with apraclonidine showed reversal of anisocoria which confirms the diagnosis. Her history of recent chiropractic manipulation and an ipsilateral headache is very concerning for carotid artery dissection which is considered a neuro-ophthalmic emergency due to the risk for CVA. MRI / MRA of the head and neck is the appropriate study to assess for carotid dissection. The treatment of carotid dissection is controversial and depends on clinician preference and the acuteness of onset. Some experts advocate anticoagulation for stroke prevention but anticoagulation is not the correct answer choice because the diagnosis of carotid dissection should be confirmed prior to initiating treatment. There are multiple types of primary headache disorders such as migraine, cluster headache, and paroxysmal hemicrania that can cause headache and Horner syndrome. Patients with these primary headache disorders would not require anticoagulation for this issue. physiologic anisocoria classically demonstrates a difference in pupil size that is equal in light and dark and the difference between the pupils measures less than how many millimeters? A.0.2 mm B.0.5 mm C.1.0 mm D.2.0 mm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Anisocoria can be appreciated reliably on clinical examination when a 0.2 mm to 0.4 mm difference in pupillary diameter occurs. The classic teaching is that physiologic anisocoria virtually always entails less than 1 mm difference in pupillary diameter (although greater disparities can occur). In cases of anisocoria greater than 1 mm, alternative diagnoses should be carefully considered. Approximately 20% of healthy individuals have anisocoria so it is often not a harbinger of "badness." Which of the following possible causes of anisocoria would be expected to result in anisocoria that is equal in dark and light? A.Carotid dissection B.Posterior communicating artery aneurysm C.Cluster headache D.Physiologic anisocoria High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The rule is that physiologic anisocoria (PA) is the same in light and dark conditions although there can be exceptions. Some cases of PA can show more pronounced anisocoria in dark lighting. In that case, cocaine testing would help distinguish PA from Horner's syndrome because both eyes will dilate equally in response to cocaine while in Horner's syndrome the abnormal smaller pupil does not respond equally to cocaine. Cluster headaches and carotid dissections can both be causes of ipsilateral Horner's syndromes and would be expected to result in an anisocoria that is greater in dark due to impaired sympathetic input on the side of the lesion causing a miotic pupil with abnormal dilation. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can cause an ipsilateral pupil involving third nerve palsy due to compressive impairment of pupillomotor fibers running in the peripheral / external portion of the third nerve. This would be expected to cause anisocoria that is greater in light conditions due to impaired parasympathetic pupillary constriction in the larger pupil. hich of the following diseases is NOT associated with paradoxical pupillary reaction? A.Duane syndrome B.Dominant optic atrophy C.Best disease D.Congenital achromatopsia Topic: The Patient with Pupillary Abnormalities High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: For unknown reasons, early onset (usually congenital) disease of optic nerve or retinal disease can result in a paradoxical pupillary reaction. Affected patients will have immediate pupillary constriction instead of dilation upon turning the exam room lights off. The finding is most significant clinically in young children with poor vision of unknown etiology. Paradoxical pupillary reaction is highly suggestive of optic nerve or retinal pathology. The full differential diagnosis for paradoxical pupillary reaction should be memorized and includes: • congenital stationary night blindness • congenital achromatopsia • Best disease • dominant optic atrophy • optic nerve hypoplasia • Leber congenital amaurosis • Albinism • retinitis pigmentosa A 30-year-old female presents with a dilated left pupil that she first noticed while applying make-up one week ago. She denies any associated diplopia or ptosis. She denies any recent eye drops, takes no medications, and has suffered no ocular trauma in the past. On examination, she has 20/20 vision OU at distance with no evidence of an afferent pupillary defect. Her right pupil measures 5 mm in the dark and 3 mm in the light while her left pupil is slightly irregular (oval), measures about 8 mm in the dark, and is sluggishly reactive to light to 7 mm. The remainder of her examination is unremarkable (including alignment and motility testing). Pilocarpine 0.125% is applied to both eyes and 30 minutes following drop administration there is no response in the right eye but dramatic constriction in the left eye to 3 mm. Which of the following findings / symptoms would NOT be expected in association with this patient's pupil disorder? A.Blurred near vision in the left eye B.Headache / periorbital pain C.Spontaneous segmental oscillations of the iris musculature in the left eye D.Light-near dissociation in the left eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A tonic pupil is caused by disruption of post-ganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers from the ciliary ganglion. While tonic pupils can rarely be associated with orbital tumors, VZV infection, orbital trauma, giant cell arteritis, diabetes, amyloidosis, and syphilis, the vast majority of the cases are idiopathic and isolated. Common findings of a tonic pupil include sluggish pupillary reactivity to light, more prominent pupillary constriction on near gaze than to light (light-near dissociation), segmental constriction (parts of iris reactive while others are not), and hypersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine (0.1% or 0.125%). Other features of tonic pupils include loss of accommodation (which is usually temporary with resolution over months) and "vermiform" spontaneous segmental oscillations of the iris musculature. Over many years, tonic pupils often "shrink" and may eventually become more miotic than the normal contralateral eye. Tonic pupils are more common in females (70% of cases) and are usually unilateral at onset (80%). The risk of contralateral tonic pupil development, however, is about 1-4% per year in unilateral cases. Tonic pupils are generally not associated with headache. Bilateral tonic pupils can occur along with diminished deep tendon reflexes as part of a syndrome known as Adies syndrome. While a this is a popular test question and pimp question, there is little clinical significance to the presence of diminished deep tendon reflexes. What is the primary mechanism of action of apraclonidine? A.Beta adrenergic receptor agonist (beta 1 > beta 2) B.Alpha adrenergic receptor agonist (alpha 2 > alpha 1) C.Alpha adrenergic receptor antagonist (alpha 1 > alpha 2) D.Beta adrenergic receptors antagonist (beta 2 > beta 1) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Apraclonidine is an alpha-adrenergic receptor agonist that has more effect on alpha-2 receptors than alpha-1 receptors. It is not completely clear how it functions in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome, but the current theory revolves around up-regulation of post-synaptic alpha-1 receptors in Horner syndrome. The belief is that as early as 36 hours following disruption of sympathetic fibers to the eye, the pupillary dilator muscle experiences up-regulation of alpha-1 receptors in response to sympathetic denervation. A normal pupillary response to apraclonidine 0.5% (trade name Iopidine) is mild constriction due to action of the medication on pre-synaptic alpha-2 receptors which act to decrease release of norepinephrine to the dilator muscle. In patients with Horner syndrome, however, the action of apraclonidine on up-regulated alpha-1 receptors predominates over the alpha-2 effect resulting in dilation. In an individual with unilateral Horner syndrome who has apraclonidine drops applied bilaterally, the sympathetically denervated eye dilates and the normal eye constricts leading to reversal of anisocoria.
